Microsoft support does not have a clue about their own product support, licensing, or how it works. Each person you talk to at Microsoft support says different things. Here are some of the fallacies I was told:
1. You can have as many licenses in your account as you need if you have 10-15 computers, notebooks, and tablets for your whole family, just add more licenses - this is not true. If you load a second or third license into your account, Microsoft extends out the expiration period a year per license, but does not allow more than 5 devices per account. So if you load three licenses you get three years for just 5 devices.
2. Each home licenses supports up to 10 devices. No; despite Microsoft support insisting the license for 5 allows ten. They are wrong a license for 5 is for 5.
3. I'll transfer you to the group that can help you. Wrong again, all Microsoft does on a transfer is hang up.
4. I can help you. No there is no Microsoft person who can help you if you make the mistake of adding two licenses to one account. All they can do is punish you for making that mistake
5. Our license agreement clearly shows that you cannot add more than one license to one account it is located at: [...] [...] [...] Wrong again; at some point they may put that there but so far no one at Microsoft can point to a page that shows that.
Regarding the Office 365, once you slog through the incompetence at Microsoft support the Office works fine, but frankly Office 2010 is more intuitive. Why does Microsoft move around functions to make them hard to find?

That was very difficult to do within the reconcile window so I had to jump back & forth between that window and my main register.  As much as I tried I could not get the account to reconcile!  At one point I changed a transaction from a payment to a deposit and then back to a payment and instead of being back to my original balance my register was off even more.  I quit.  It was a waste of $60+!  Stick with the PC version or find something else until Quicken can fix the problems.

I am also a long time Quicken user. I tried the upgrade to Quicken 2012, and reverted back to 2010 almost immediately because I could not use the budgeting functionality. I decided to give Quicken 2013 a try, and at first it seemed that many of the 2012 budgeting issues were resolved. But then I made a mistake - I turned on \\"Detailed Loan Payments\\", and all of a sudden the actual totals in my budget were no longer correct. So I turned that off, and instead tried to budget by using the pieces of the loan payment (including the transfer to the loan account - I want my budget to reflect cash flow). Wow was that a mistake! Now nothing totals correctly, budget totals, actual totals, or balances. The numbers are completely useless. The most basic reason I use budget software is so I don't have to get out my calculator, and here I am, using a calculator! So I have reverted my budget to an excel spreadsheet, just like I used to do 15 years ago. This is extremely disappointing, especially since Intuit seems to think its OK to charge to upgrade each year, and yet the software is nowhere near ready for release. I agree with the other reviewers who basically said \\"I did not pay to be a beta tester!\\".

In addition to a total fail in functionality, the budget feature is also dreadfully cumbersome. If you have your categories organized into groups, everything is automatically expanded for you every time you change the display view, and if you want to just see a summary, you are constantly manually closing every group. This is very annoying. The graph view of the budget is also pretty useless. You get a huge red bar if you miss your budget by .01. Somehow the visual display needs to reflect relative importance of an item. Missing by .01 is not the same as missing by 1000. So even the attempt at giving you visual clues to help analyze the budget status are poor.

Now I'm debating whether or not to revert to 2010, but at this point, that would take a lot of time, I would have to go back to my last 2010 backup and reenter a bunch of stuff. My Excel budget I set up will work, but it makes me angry that I paid for this upgrade, and now I have to do my budget by hand again. I can't believe Intuit has slipped this far and for so long. Its pretty clear that Quicken is no longer a product they care about. Or maybe they think that their customer base is so stupid they won't notice that the budget totals are wrong!

So bottom line - if you are new to financial software, and wanting to try getting a handle on your finances, DO NOT BUY QUICKEN. 3 stars is fair because some things are fair and some things are poor with Streets and Trips. I am a field sales person, and I have 400 customers who are points on the map that I have to figure out who to visit everyday. I am a heavy map user - I've been using Streets and Trips for more than a decade, and I use MapPoint (Microsofts other map tool) for territory design (splitting up the territories between reps in the first place), and the Badger Map for building my daily schedule and organizing my territory.    First, the Good about Streets and Trips.    1. You can use it offline. This is the most important part for me, because there are parts of my territory that are our of service. When I'm in service, I use the Badger Map to plan my day and route on my ipad, but when AT&T doesn't feel like building towers, I whip out my trusty laptop and get on Streets and Trips.  2. Streets and Trips beats all the handhelds hands down. It allows me to get granular manipulate my routes and choose routes in a way that you can't with the handhelds. I need this for my job.  3. The new version allows me to change and manipulate icons and filter them off the map beautifully. Huge upgrade over past versions.  4. The display of the map and the scheme/legend clear and clean. A great job and helps organize. It would be great if I could change the order in the legend to prioritize and make it make more sense.  5. The point of interest icons are great, and help me find things like hotels when I don't have an internet connection  6. Maybe the best part about S&T is that the Multiple Destination routing (Offline). I sometimes have 10 points in a day if I'm out prospecting. Being able to sort and organize my stops in the best order and get directions from one stop to next is awesome.  7. S&T works great - easy to install. I see that a lot of people had problems installing S&T and getting it to work in the first place. I don't have that problem, I have a Lenovo Thinkpad that is about 3 years old.    And now The Problems with Streets and Trips    1. Why can't I interact with my iPhone, what about my iPad? The fact that this is just on my computer is probably the biggest limitation. I need a send to iPhone feature. especially since the GPX export doesn't work - which brings me to...gripe #2  2. When I export to GPX files (which I want to do because I'm going to be offline), the files are corrupt. I've checked all over the forums, this seems to be happening to lots of people. I have to punch the addresses into my Garmin manually. not the end of the world though.  3. The road maps are pretty weak. They are just years behind on changes. luckily since I'm mostly using this in places that are offline - and those places don't change as much, this doesn't hurt much.  4. I regularly run into problems if I don't get the street name absolutely perfect. sometimes things like Lane instead of Ln etc will throw it off.  5. This is an important one for sales people, but probably less important for people trying to design their vacation. I have to upload my customer lists, and those lists have attributes, like customer type, sales information, etc. This is pretty bad in S&T, and if you want to change anything, you have to start over. This keeps you from using this as a place to take notes and interact with customer data.  6. With every edition of Streets and Trips you are starting from Scratch. When I tried to load my old maps, from earlier versions of S&T, it didn't work.  7. Google Maps has a ton of features that Streets and Trips does not. It looks like since Streets and Trips is discontinued, Microsoft has admitted the war is lost here. Which is a real shame, because Streets and Trips does so much that Google does not do. Walking directions, the great traffic info, a rich database of points of interest, public transport, information on where the coffee shops are so I don't fall asleep at the wheel... all missing in S&T.ops are so I don’t fall asleep at the wheel… all missing in S&T.

For instance, the auto formatting function has its pros and cons. It makes your script look professional, but there are lots of irritating problems. Like you can't add an extra empty line between lines: if you press Enter you bring up the Element box. Also when you finish typing a character name and want to add parentheses, you can't just manually type them in, you have to bring them up from the drop down menu, otherwise Final Draft treats it as dialogue and when you press Enter it defaults to Action. The save PDF function is just broken: if you've already saved a draft and then want to overwrite it, you can't, you have to change the file name or delete the previous file first; even that sometimes doesn't work, for reasons I've never been able to find out. PowerPoint and Excel: No crashing or functionality problems, but I also have not discovered any real advantages over 2008. Perhaps there are some, but I haven't stumbled into them. These are neutral, but I still miss the very functional Formatting Palette.

Outlook: Connecting to Exchange server was easy and it works fine. I have had no issues with my IMAP accounts, and the Calendar works especially well. This is a nice upgrade from Entourage.

Norton Security for one device is the latest incarnation of what was Norton Internet Security. Norton has revamped their retail security lineup with the home line simplified to pretty much Norton Security with or without backup.

Just ONE Please...:
This item has licensing for just ONE Windows, Mac, IOS (iPhone/iPad) or Android device. If you ONLY have one device this is fine, but if you have even two you are much better getting the 5 device version of [[ASIN:B00MHZ6Z64 Norton Security]] or 10 device [[ASIN:B00MHZ71G2 Norton Security with Backup]] which should be enough for many families.

Whether you get the 1, 5 or 10 device license version it is the same product. Depending on the device there are differing feature sets. For example, IOS devices get no antivirus. I have Windows and IOS so I'll share my experience with these.

Windows Setup:
Windows Installation was faster than with older versions of Norton and was pretty painless for me. I did have to restart my Windows 7 Pro desktop. The controls available are pretty basic and there are lots of on/off controls to customize how Norton works. What is hard to find in this incarnation of Norton Security is the ability to white-list specific directories or files. This caused some consternation for me until I finally found it deep in the settings.

In operation on Windows I feel Norton Security is less "noisy" than previous versions; I don't feel like I'm constantly being marketed to death. Unlike previous versions of the retail product I didn't perceive my PC running noticeably slower with it in operation. This is a very good thing! The initial full scan turned up a couple of minor items missed by my previous antivirus, but none of these were active viruses. Instead they were inactive left over pieces of already removed viruses.

Application Compatibility Problems:
I use VirtualBox to run a virtual machine on this PC. When I installed Norton Security Virtualbox was unable to start my virtual machine instance. Virtual box seems to have problems with most recent Symantec antivirus products (including [[ASIN:B00JKZPTPC Norton Small Business]]). I was stuck until I upgraded VirtualBox to a version which is newer than the latest official release (as of Oct. 1, 2014). This virtual machine is critical to my business so I was happy to finally resolve this. This is the only application compatibility problem I've come across so far.

NOTE: As of Late February Virtual Box seems to work fine again with the mainstream releases IF you disable Norton Security during installation.

How About Norton Security WITH Backup:
If you want an integrated on-line backup solution or have more than 5 devices, you might want to consider getting [[ASIN:B00MHZ71G2 Norton Security with Backup]] it supports 10 devices and includes 25GB of online backup space. Windows 7 Pro has a very capable backup program that works well with USB or network drives as backup media. The difference in price it might be well spent if you need online backup and/or more than 5 devices.

Mobile Support:
The IOS app is a disappointment to me. It has a few features which do not include any virus protection:
1) locate your phone: this placed my iPhone 4 a over a mile away from its actual location!!
2) it can ring your phone: I can just dial the number...
3) it has a "scream" function: makes your iPhone put out an annoying siren like noise

If the "scream" actually sounded like a scream this app would at least have some entertainment value. If you have more devices than the 10 allowed in this product, don't waste one on an IOS device! The IOS support is pretty poor. I have read that Android devices have better support against malware, but I don't have an android device to try this out.

Conclusions:
This incarnation of Symantec's Norton line of retail/home security products is pretty good overall but has some issues. It finds things other antivirus solutions on my Windows 7 Pro PC did not and does not seem to slow things down for me. I had one application with a problem, but nothing else. Mobile support for iPhone/iPad is poor. The user interface is simple, but buries the advanced controls deep in the settings.

Overall Norton Security should be a good tradeoff for most home users.

The ONE device license is not a bargain. These days, who has just one device?

The software itself is a great product for most people. If you have more than 1 device get the 5 device version or the 10 device version if more than 5 or you want backup too.

Because of the minor issues and relatively poor value compared to the multi-device Norton Security versions I'm giving Norton Security for 1 device just 3 stars.

* No good plumbing plan - Not able to create a useful plumbing plan

I bought this program as opposed to using "non architectural" 3D cad for the following reasons:

1. Shortcut in design. I wanted to be able to plop in windows and doors without going nuts modeling everything.
2. Get an idea of what some standard dimensions are. I don't want to try to figure out how tall an actual finished roof is.
3. Get materials lists, etc.

What I found is that for a relatively simple house (single story), designing from scratch is easy. Try to change *anything*, and you're in for a world of hurt. You'll end up with the house floating over your yard, or sunken in, or the foundation shows over your floors... You need to refer to the documentation often if you want to get things "just right".

The built in library of furniture is hideous. I'm sure you can spend hours attempting to make it match what you actually want to put in your house but in the end I just put in the same dimensions as the cabinets I wanted just to plan the size of the room. That means my interior views are by no means what the house will look like.

Generally speaking, there are many ways for the user to get punished if he doesn't think ahead. I started messing around designing a house and then I wanted to add the lot later... good luck. You start with the surveyor's maps and you can (if you read the documentation) enter lines in the "so many feet along this direction" notation they use. Then of course your lot will end up with north facing up. Want to now rotate the whole thing (including north arrow) so that your side lot line is horizontal? Good luck. Want to move chunks of a house? You will inevitably break something.

The navigation in a 3D view is an atrocity. In the plan view, you can insert a camera somewhere and quickly get a 3D view. Trying to now move this camera around as if you were standing there moving your head is a nightmare. You try to pan around with the middle button and usethe mouse wheel to zoom in and out but in fact it is changing camera parameters like focal length. You'll end up with a fisheye lens view of a single window and wonder how the @#$%@ to get back... you close the window and start over, that's how. They give you "dolly" (pan along the ground), "tilt" (as if your body were still and you could only move your head) and "pan" (which is only altitude and side to side); to simply "look around a room" takes using all three *carefully* because, for example, the "dolly" resets the tilt and seems to attempt to not crash into furniture and walls (but you end up looking at your studs somehow anyway).

For a remodel, things get worse. You try to replicate your house and things become very difficult. You cannot simply draw a dimension, type in a number, and have something move. Instead you can click on things and some dimensions appear which you can change---but the behavior of *what* moves when you change the dimension is not clear, so you end up with battles of you put the first window relative to the door and then you go try to move the second window and instead the first window moves back. And sometimes you click and the dimension you want doesn't appear. So you click, and click, and click here, and there, and sometimes you get lucky.

Roof geometry is very complicated. I have to say the automatic roofing on this thing is like magic. But you better like what it gives you. If you are adding a room to your house and you want to put in the existing roof to see how to best extend it to the addition - good luck! There's some built in adjustments to try to get roof planes to line up but again you end up with things moving around in circles until nothing matches anymore. That is, you cannot "fix" a part of your house so it cannot be changed. Anything you want to keep exactly as in your measurements will have to be double-checked often. I feel like if they just let youdrag the points defining the planes around in 3D you'd get around all these troubles, but that's not possible.

So, I "don't like it". I feel like it takes months to work on a design because I get frustrated easily and have to take a break. The creative process is often interrupted by trying to figure out how something can be done. What this is is a full-fledged CAD program which people probably take a long time to master but "dumbed down" so that they can charge less. It's not clear to me if the dumbing down is what makes this so bad, or if it's the underlying CAD causing the problems.

Because let's face it - $500 (or $2000) is well worth it if it replaces hiring someone to do your drawings on a big project.

If you want to fantasize about your dream home, I suggest you spend the money on some drawing classes instead. You'll get your results much faster.

I downloaded the trial version of Elements 13 to see if it was worth purchasing the key code and upgrading my Version 12. Here's what I found out.

Help: ELive gives you some selected methods for removing \\"pet eye\\", editing batches of photos, using Facebook and some other frequently desired tasks. There are three new Guided Edits for black-and-white procesesing. There is an improved method to cut out and merge people or things from one photo to another. (Photomerge Compose.)
The Organizer has been changed a bit, to give it a look similar to many online image organizers--you can adjust the thumbnail view of your image as you scroll through them in the Organizer.

As usual, Photoshop Elements is a large program and somewhat slow. I reviewed Corel Paintshop Pro XL earlier and the difference in the amount of disk space they take up is astonishing: Photoshop Elements uses 3.5 gigabytes of disk space while Corel's PaintShop only uses 200 Megabytes (that's a lot smaller.) I found the Corel program was a lot faster to load and use.

The actually changes to version 13 are \\"under the hood\\" and not as visible to the average user: Elements 13 now supports high-DPI displays. So should you upgrade? Unless you have had a problem with large edits in the past, I'd say if you have Version 12, this is not worth the upgrade. If you have upgraded your PC system recently and have an older version (11 and back) then yes, this is worthwhile.

This does not apply to you if you only have one account on your Mac.  However if you run multiple users on the Mac read on, as you may have the problem described below.  A few years ago I documented installation problems H&R Block has when you run multi-user on Macs (which you should as a good security practice).  That review is here: [[ASIN:B002SR4S0Q H&R Block At Home 2009 Deluxe Federal + State + eFile [OLD VERSION]]]  Although it's better, there is still one problem that may be difficult or impossible for most non-techie sorts to figure out on their own.  It has to do with State program installation.  The problem and the solution is below:  I always install programs as root or Administrator to ensure file permissions are all OK.  (Indeed not doing so in past years caused problems with H&R Block).  Once installed (both the Federal and the State plug-in) I switch back to a normal non-privileged user to run all of my programs to include H&R Block.  The problem occurred when I wanted to start the state program. Although I had successfully downloaded and installed the state plug-in as root/Admin (in my case Maryland) when I tried to access it as my normal user it said I did not have a state program installed, and offered to let me buy one!  Here's how you have to solve the problem:  Sign back in as root/Admin.  Using the Finder navigate down to Library/Application Support/H&RBlock/H&RBlock 2011/Completed Updates/ then copy the file xx.TCstate11 where xx is the two-letter abbreviation for your state.  (In my case that was the MD.TCstate11 file).  Using Finder navigate to a shared directory that can be accessed by both users, e.g. Macintosh HD/Users/Shared and paste a copy of that file into that shared directory.  Go back to your normal user and sign in again.  Navigate to the Macintosh HD/Users/Shared directory and find your xx.TCstate11 file.  Using another Finder window navigate down to your home directory then the directory Library/Application Support/H&RBlock/H&RBlock 2011/Completed Updates/  (I had to create the Completed Updates directory in my normal user account as it did not exist yet).  Copy (or move) the xx.TCstate11 file into the directory above.  Double click that xx.TCstate11 file. A .dmg mountable file appears.  Double click on that too, and a state installer pop-up appears, which then redownloads your already-paid-for state program and inserts it as a plug-in to your normal user account library profile.  You're good to go.  This is annoying especially since I reported similar multi-user install problems in past years to H&R Block.  Apparently they still haven't gotten that bug worked out.  Sigh.  Anyway, this would be a five star review without that installation bug that affects some users, but two stars got deducted for not fixing a known flaw that has been known by them for two years.  (I called and wrote the company documenting it in addition to my Amazon reviews.)

I bought this for the anti-virus. Kaspersky has been at or near the top of antivirus rankings for years. In this, I was not disappointed. My first scan turned up a few things left behind by my old antivirus (Avast), it runs quickly, and the real-time scanning is unobtrusive.

I'm not fond of some of the extras that come along with it though. They really could have done a much better job.

The "Safe Money" app seemed interesting, but it does not integrate with very many browsers. I use Opera, which has nothing at all from Kaspersky available. Chrome recently disabled all extensions not found on Google's app store, and Kaspersky has not fixed that, so Chrome is a no-go. I don't use Firefox or IE but I did notice IE had something going on with Kaspersky. There were some other extensions that came along as well, but as I said I use Opera so I'm not really sure what they would give me.

The parental protection stuff is a joke. Web filtering works; but adding exceptions does NOT work. I had to disable web filtering entirely to allow Netflix. Very disappointing. Access restriction controls, which supposedly allow locking specific users out of the computer during certain times (a.k.a. "bedtime enforcer") dutifully return to the login screen if the computer is on during that time. But the user can log back in and dismiss the Kaspersky dialog. Completely worthless.

The various scans have very flexible scheduling, which I like. But I don't see an option to pause the scan if the computer is in use. There was once I came back from vacation and immediately the scan started (because the computer had been off, it missed the scheduled scan), making me unable to use the computer until I figured out what was going on, then explored the menus until I found the "pause scan" button. There was no nice right-click menu on the task bar to pause the scan or see if it was running like I've seen in other AV products. Once I had the scan paused (at 94%) I accidentally hit the "start scan" button that looks like a "play" button on a music player. That restarted the scan from 0% instead of resuming the paused scan. You do that with some link-looking text. Not very clear UI at all.

All in all, I'm mostly satisfied...but I may shop around looking at reviews of other products when the time is up, looking for more functional extras or better UI.

After observing and reading reviews here since December (2013) when Intuit's nasty gram arrived about the requirement to update, I was apprehensive about updating from Quicken Premier 2011 to Quicken Premier 2014. I also started giving more weight to the most recent reviews here on Amazon as I felt those would reflect improvements in what certainly appears to have been a buggy and premature release last Fall. My primary use of Quicken is on a desktop, however I have Q 2011 installed on my laptop to fall back on.

I used the Quicken Premier 2014 download link supplied by Amazon. When I completed downloading the installer, I did not let it run. Instead I saved it to my hard disk so that I have a copy to retain. I also copied the downloaded installer to a thumbdrive to archive it, as I have done for previous versions of Quicken.

I then ran the installer to install on my desktop. I had no idea what release version the 2014 installer was installing. The installation process clearly looks for updates, but again, I did not trust how complete that may be during the installation process. So once the installation process was complete, I allowed it to start Quicken Premier 2014. However at that point I did not allow it to open my current data file when it prompted me to do so. Instead I had Quicken start without loading any data file. Then from that state, I had Quicken update itself again. I am not sure if at that point it found any additional updates, but I had read to do this in a couple of other reviews. I then closed Quicken and then restarted it. I checked Help - About Quicken and it showed Release R 7 (32.1.7.6) was installed. I confirmed it to be the latest release. Then buoyed by the fact that I had my laptop with Q 2011 to fall back on, I allowed it to convert my desktop's data file to 2014 format.

My conversion went smoothly. I worked through all of my accounts looking for any discrepancies, using my laptop with 2011 and the same data file prior to conversion as my baseline. I found no discrepancies. I then performed an Update cycle on each of the two computers to update my investment portfolio on both the desktop (Q 2014) and laptop (Q 2011), and then again compared. Again, Quicken 2014 was spot on with Quicken 2011. The only issues I had were that Q 2014 found and attemptedto update historical price information on about three mutual funds that I am no longer invested in, and whose names and ticker symbols had changed since I last invested in them. Quicken provides the ability to uncheck those, preventing any additional attempts to update them.

Note on importance of archiving financial files:
When I started a new file with Quicken Premier 2011 at the start of 2014, I set my date range to retain transactions from January 1, 2012 to the current date at that time. So the file I was working with that was converted to Q 2014 is for calendar year 2012, 2013, and 2014 to-date. That allows me also to easily search for transactions that occurred during that range.

I am absolutely astounded at those who have stated in their reviews that they lost years of transactions due to faulty conversion by Quicken 2014. I keep my older versions of Quicken, either the installation DVD/CD's or installation downloads. I always make multiple backups of current and prior year(s) Quicken data files as Intuit always insists on converting prior Quicken version data files to each new Quicken version. Before converting I keep one copy of the data file in its normal location, and I make backups to at least two separate places; usually one to a separate hard drive and another to a thumbdrive. I usually accumulate up to 3 years at a time in my current Quicken file, and at that point archive the file(s) in case I need to go back later to do research on something. I rename the archive file(s) so that the filename clearly indicates the years covered. Obviously, if I need to go back let's say five years, the pertinent file will be from a previous Quicken version. When it comes time to do any research in an archived file, I always make sure I have two additional copies before I allow Quicken to convert one of them to a new release's format. So I always have copies to fall back on if needed.

Perspective on how I use Quicken Premier:
I have somewhat of a financial background, and to an extent I am \\"old school\\" when it comes to finances. I have a very complex investment portfolio and rely heavily on daily downloads of transactions and price history for the investments, which are spread among several investment brokerages. The number of transactions involved is considerable and they would be very time consuming to enter manually. To have Quicken Premier keep my brokerage accounts up to date and accurate is a must for me. And I do about once a week log into those accounts on the brokerage web sites and verify the balances. Quicken Premier 2014 has been 100% accurate, just as was Quicken Premier 2011.

On the other hand, in regard to banking and credit card transactions, I am very much different. I do not even consider use of Quicken's Update for those accounts. There is usually a lag between the day the transaction occurs and the date it gets posted at the bank or credit institution.

I also have a large number of Quicken Categories and do a lot of split transactions; splits which cannot be done via Quicken updates. So I do not rely in any way on any Quicken downloads for bank or credit card accounts.

Example: I want to know how much I spend on Groceries, not how much I spent in grocery stores. There are a lot of items available in grocery stores that are not groceries; and a lot of groceries available in stores like Target and Walmart who are not classified as grocery stores. I'd say I create split transactions for more than half of my spending receipts.

Another example: I track how much I pay in Sales Tax for income tax deduction purposes.

So when I write a check, use a credit card, or use a debit card, I keep the receipts and post the transactions to Quicken myself, manually. For routine monthly bills, such as phone and utility bills and the like, when the bill arrives I schedule payments through the online banking at my credit union's web site, and I schedule them in Quicken as well, and have Quicken notify me 2 business days in advance of the upcoming payments. And I routinely glance at my upcoming scheduled transactions to make sure I have them covered.

And yes, I still maintain a written register in my checkbook.......

Norton Security single device license version of the latest incarnation of what was Norton Internet Security. Norton has revamped their retail security lineup with the home line simplified to pretty much Norton Security with or without backup.

This has licensing for just ONE device: Windows, Mac, IOS (iPhone/iPad) or Android. If you ONLY have one device this is fine, but if you have even two you are much better getting the 5 device version of [[ASIN:B00MHZ6Z64 Norton Security]] or 10 device [[ASIN:B00MHZ71G2 Norton Security with Backup]] which should be enough for many families.

In either 1, 5 or 10 device licenses you do not get the same features on all devices. I have Windows and IOS so I'll share my experience with these.

Windows Setup:

Windows Installation was faster than with older versions of Norton and was pretty painless for me. I did have to restart my Windows 7 Pro desktop. The controls available are pretty basic and there are lots of on/off controls to customize how Norton works. What is missing in this incarnation of Norton Security is the ability to white-list specific directories or files. This caused some consternation for me, but more on that near the end.

In operation on Windows I feel Norton Security is less \\"noisy\\" than previous versions; I don't feel like I'm constantly being marketed to death. Unlike previous versions of the retail product I didn't perceive my PC running noticeably slower with it in operation. This is a very good thing! The initial full scan turned up a couple of minor items missed by my previous antivirus, but none of these were active viruses. Instead they were inactive left over pieces of already removed viruses.

Application Compatibility Problems:

I use VirtualBox to run a virtual machine on this PC. When I installed Norton Security Virtualbox would not start my virtual machine instance. Virtual box seems to have problems with most recent Symantec antivirus products (including [[ASIN:B00JKZPTPC Norton Small Business]]). I was stuck until I upgraded VirtualBox to a version which is newer than the latest official release (as of Oct. 1, 2014). It was good I found a solution because this virtual machine is critical to my business. This was the only application compatibility problem I've come across so far.

Since then I found the settings for exclusions. It isn't on the security page reached via the advanced button as one might expect, but found from the small gear icon for settings at the top of the control panel. The exclusions are buried in this group of settings pages. Go to settings, antivirus, scans tab, to Exclusions/Low Risks and then finally items to exclude.

If you want an integrated on-line backup solution, you might want to consider getting [[ASIN:B00MHZ71G2 Norton Security with Backup]] that supports 10 devices and includes 25GB of online backup space. Windows 7 Pro has a very capable backup program that works well with USB or network drives as backup media. For the difference in price it might be well spent if you need online backup and/or more than 5 devices.

Mobile Support:

The IOS app is a disappointment to me. It has a few features which do not include any virus protection:
1) locate your phone: this placed my iPhone 4 a mile way from its actual location!!
2) it can ring your phone: I can just dial the number
3) it has a \\"scream\\" function: makes your iPhone put out an annoying siren like noise

If the \\"scream\\" actually sounded like a scream this app would at least have some entertainment value. If you have more devices than the 10 allowed in this product, don't waste one on an IOS device! The IOS support is pretty lame. I have read that Android devices have better support against malware, but I don't have an android device to try this out.

Conclusions:

This incarnation of Symantec's Norton line of retail/home security products is pretty good. It finds things other antivirus solutions on this computer did not, and does not seem to slow things down. I had one application that had a problem, but nothing else. Mobile support for iPhone/iPad is poor. The user interface is simple, but does not include some advanced controls like white listing of applications, files or folders. It is probably a good tradeoff for most home users.

The ONE device license is not a bargain. The software itself is a great product for most people. I had an application problem and the IOS app is poor. This has been my first year of using H&R Block software after many, many years of using Turbo Tax. After finally completing my tax return, here is a more or less complete review, based on my experience: 1. Overall, the H&R software did the job, and was less expensive than TT. Download, installation and several upgrades (Federal, State and software itself) did not cause any problems in my Windows 7 environment. The online help has been adequate; menus/navigation and user interface are a little bit confusing and counterintuitive, but this may just need a little bit of getting used to. Importing of the previous year tax return (TT file) was easy, with a single exception – H&R software failed to import one of the carryover deductions (deductible points from the mortgage refinancing a few years ago – this amount is spread over the life of the loan, and TT picks it up every year without a problem).  2. Preparation of the tax return (both Federal and State) was fairly simple and straightforward. Some of the interview questions were not simple (for me) to answer, so I had to look for online help (it was not very helpful) and search Internet (oddly, the best and clearest answers came from the Intuit web site) . This year my tax liabilities were (expectedly so) a bit higher than usual, and the software nicely walked me through the estimate of the penalties for Federal tax return (which ended up being minimal). However, for the State tax return, I was asked a few fairly cryptic questions and then a State form was shown, and I was asked to fill it in. Well, do I really need H&R software to fill in tax forms manually? This was not a big dial, so I filled the form in, and then the software estimated the penalty (ended up being $0).  3. I finally E-filed the Federal tax return without any issues; then I paper-filed the State return. All the forms were printed nicely, I liked the option of selecting which forms to print or save in PDF for archiving, and whether to include or nor the worksheets and checklist. The software worked well preparing backup copies of the tax return, in both H&R and PDF formats. I missed the feature which TT has – comparing my financials with the rest of the population in my income category; this is a feature that H&R could easily add.  4. As happens (to me) almost every year, one of the investment accounts sent an amended 1099-DIV after I have filed the 2014 returns. Normally, it would take me about 15 minutes in TT to prepare amended Federal and State returns, and send them (on paper) for processing. It became quite an adventure with H&R software. For Federal return, I had to go through a number of not very intuitive and often manual steps to create, print and assemble an amended return (and I am still not sure that I assembled it right - H&R should be better in saying which forms/schedules got changed and need to be re-submitted). Goof news is that it was created, printed, and sent. For State, the only thing I received from the software was a message that Form 502X (amended return for my state) is not included with this software, but I can download it from my state web site, fill it manually, and send it to the State tax authorities. Which I did – and why would I need H&R software if I ended up doing all of this manually?  At this point, I am giving this product rating of “3” (meaning "it's OK"), and next year I will think whether to stay with H&R or switch back to TT.

I don't have anything to add that hasn't already been said in some of the thousands of comments.  I hope Intuit fixes this for tax year 2015 and the lesson sticks for future years.  This isn't the first time Intuit has tried to pull a fast one on customers and been caught.  There was a TT controversy a few years ago about printing additional tax returns.  And Quicken/Quickbooks - the file format changes with every new version, so once you upgrade you can't go back and you become a slave to whatever mandatory bundled services come with the new version.  And every upgrade seems to have more required services bundled in.  One good one - with Quickbooks, the Intuit self-service payroll service is only good for three years.  If you're a Quickbooks customer and you use Quickbooks for payroll, even self-serve payroll - you must upgrade to the new version every 3 years to keep getting payroll updates.  But this review is for Turbotax Deluxe, not all the other Intuit products.  And for me, overall, it worked.  I called the toll free number early and Intuit gave me a free upgrade to Premier, so I was able to deal with my Schedule E and Schedule K1.  That worked.  The installation went smoothly, the interviews asked all the right questions and, near as I can tell, all the forms looked good.  I e-filed my federal taxes and US Mailed my state taxes.  A text message came to my cell phone a few hours after e-filing that it was received, so the process was smooth.  If I have to install TT on some other computer in the future and do something with my 2014 taxes, that will be a problem - but it's unlikely.  And I have PDFs of all the forms.  Finally, there's Turbotax VP Bob Meighan.  Bobhas been the public point man through all this and he's taken a great deal of abuse.  Kudos to Bob for staying engaged and mixing it up, even in hostile territory.  So overall - the software did its job and was easy to install and use.  Bob Meighan is a visible spokesperson and he gives the best answers he can give, at least with product functionality related issues.  That's worth five stars. I've been using Quicken on and off for probably about 20 years. My last Quicken purchase was the 2010 Starter edition--I switched back to Quicken after having abandoned it in favor of GnuCash for a few years. I didn't buy the Deluxe edition because, honestly, the Starter edition does everything I want to do that any version of Quicken is capable of doing--managing my various bank and credit card accounts. I don't really need it to manage loan accounts, and it's incapable of budgeting the way I'd like to, which would be biweekly instead of monthly. C'mon, Intuit--how much longer are you going to ignore those of us who get paid biweekly? (Luckily, the Calendar feature of Quicken provides enough insight into spending that I can use that--I enter all my recurring transactions as reminders, estimating things like groceries and gas and other things I know I'll spend money on, and the calendar shows me how much money is projected to be left in my account on any given day. Good enough.)

So, this morning Quicken 2010 warned me that after April of this year I'd no longer be able to download transactions from my financial institutions unless I upgraded to Quicken 2013. I shouldn't have been surprised--Intuit has been sticking it to its users like this for years, and we continue to put up with it because Quicken is really the only game in town. But just to stick it to us a little more, I couldn't just buy the 2013 Starter edition. Only the Deluxe edition (or higher) would import my existing Quicken data. The Starter edition is only for those who are brand-new to Quicken. So, with gritted teeth I upgraded to Quicken 2013 Deluxe, purchasing the download version here on Amazon.

The software download and subsequent installation went very smoothly. Quicken Deluxe 2013 seamlessly imported my existing data, and when it finally opened for the first time, things looked pretty-much the same as they had in my previous version. That was good enough for me.

Once installed, I explored the application a bit, customizing it for my own needs. I have to say I found little feature-wise that would have compelled me to purchase this upgrade absent the forced obsolescence of my previous version. The one thing I hoped might make it worth the upgrade was the new mobile app and cloud syncing. I created my Quicken Cloud account and synced my accounts, installed the Android app, logged in on my phone, and allowed the Quicken mobile app to sync with my cloud account. Once synced, the opening screen of the mobile app showed me account summary numbers that didn't make any sense to me. I checked my checking account balance and found that it was wildly different than what showed in Quicken on my PC. (I also noticed that both versions showed my online balance to be greatly different than what my bank showed, so that might be related to this problem.) Try as I might, I could never get my mobile app to show balances that were consistent with my PC app. That makes the mobile app completely worthless to me.

[Update on the mobile app: I decided to try one more time with the mobile app. The ending balance it shows for my checking account is still wrong -- it's off by an amount equal to the value of the one transaction that still shows as pending when I view it on my bank's web site. I'd already entered that transaction manually into Quicken Desktop, For some reason the mobile app doesn't know that and is subtracting it from my ending balance (which Quicken Desktop had already done).]

So, no compelling new features in the PC app. A worthless mobile app that shows incorrect information. Quicken 2013 Deluxe gives me absolutely nothing new for the fifty-some bucks I spent, other than the privilege of continuing to be able to download data from my financial institutions. If it weren't for that, I'd still be using my Quicken 2010 Starter edition. The only good thing I can say about Quicken Deluxe 2013 is that it allows me to doeverything I was doing with 2010 Starter. But nothing more.

I knew the day would come when I'd need to abandon Money and go to Quicken (now the only real PC option) and it came to pass early this year when my personal Money file became corrupted. Fortunately Quicken was able to convert the file, but I was left with the unpleasant task of trying to learn the more difficult Quicken interface. I still struggle to do simple things after a few months of use. I'm giving it 3stars because it works, but I never enjoy using it like I did Money... it's always aggravating. I have no intention of using mobile devices and cloud services with financial or medical data in the near future (see comments below), so am not evaluating those features.

Pros:
* It had no issues with importing a very large Money file going back >10yrs and having several accounts. That was hugely important.
* It seems able to do the basic functions needed, albeit with difficulty (for me).
* The bank account downloading heuristics (Renaming Rules) seem to work pretty well after a while, properly translating entries into my categories and payees once I figured out the interface that seems to randomly pop up. It seems to work more by magic than something I control.

Cons:
* It's more awkward to use than the Money interface, not just different.
* It truncated some Money Categories & Payees, else didn't translate them correctly, and required manual inspection to fix... very time-consuming.
* There are no Payee tools that make sense or do what I want. I don't understand this fundamental gap. I miss being able to easily change the name of a Payee on multiple entries like I could in Money, esp to make them all the same. The provided Memorized Payee function makes no sense that I can understand and doesn't seem to do anything useful. Maybe someday that mystery will be solved but I've spent hours fiddling with no breakthroughs. It's just weird.
* I've had occasions of bank account entries not downloadingat all and required hand entry. This can only be caught and fixed using statement reconciliation.
* I can't directly store a backup copy on a network disk as I could with Money; all backups must go to a child directory to Quicken data files on the local system. I don't like the vulnerability this forces me into for such relatively critical data, and it certainly isn't a necessary restriction.

Cloud & Mobile: As a long-time computing professional I have limited confidence in the first generation Cloud services being offered, as well as mobile platforms and their relatively poor integrity and security for such critical data. I will be waiting for these to mature before using for financial and medical services despite the push to do so. It is hardly surprising that vendors are having issues getting the applications and infrastructure to work properly, and customers are frustrated when it doesn't. Early adopters enjoy both the benefits and aggravation of such major changes in computing applications and services... that's the price of being a mobile-device pathfinder today. You can and should let the providers/vendors know when things don't work, but this is a heavy lift for a lot of interrelated services and is going to take a while to sort out.

I recently purchased Quicken software to import my bank statements for tax season. It was a very cumbersome process trying to figure out how to import old bank statements because many banks only offer 90 days of the file that you need to import into Quicken. Quicken has discontinued its use of the QIF file and you cannot import CSV (the format my bank uses for older statements). The only file format that Quicken will import with little problem is the QFX file format.

After a lot of web-surfing, trial and error, and reading threads in support and forum communities, I was finally able to come up with a workaround for the situation. There is a company called Propersoft who makes a bunch of converters for this type of situation. The specific program that I purchased was the CSV2QFX program. Be sure you buy the CSV2QFX and not the CSV2OFX program for Quicken. OFX is another file format and is not compatible with Quicken.

The program will set you back $40 but it is well worth it considering the headache I went through trying to figure out a way around this issue. The problem is I am really only going to use the program once because after I have all of my statements imported, I can update all of my bank data on a regular basis inside Quicken. You would think that this type of solution would be intuitive for a company named Intuit.

Transactions can be easily entered on my iPhone and updated at some later point into the main program. The investment mobile app also works well and stays updated with the main program (unlike general financial information which is stored and updated locally, investment information is stored with IGG Software when using the mobile investment App.)
I will say there are a few issues I do have with the software. First, "reports" are a necessary and important part of the program for reviewing financial information which can not be found anyplace else. Unfortunately they are very limited and somewhat inflexible. I would very much like to see a simpler, more robust report system and access to additional information outside the "report system". Second, I have so far had significant difficulty trying to set up a reasonable and useful budget. Part of the problem seems to be associated with double nested categories and seems to be made more difficult by trying to exclude certain accounts and categories from the budget. As it stands right now I basically don't use the budget, which is fine for my situation. If budgeting is a key issue and you have numerous accounts and categories I might look elsewhere. And finally, The program keeps all cash separate from stocks, mutual funds and other investments. Basically, for accounts which contain both cash and investments, I essentially have two accounts. This does make keeping track of things a little more difficult, especially when you are making trades in and out of cash within a single account. I am not a frequent trader so this is just more of a comment than a concern for me.
Overall, I am very happy with the program for my specific situation. I am hoping for eventual improvements in the reports and budget portions of the program but have now officially left Quicken behind.

As far as reviews go for years I've benefited from reading the reviews on Amazon and truly have been influenced on my purchases by all those comments and thought it was time to pay back for all those reviews I've read without contributing so I'm trying to step-it-up and write more of my own. There are many different ideas on the best way for adults to learn a foreign language. Much depends on the student, their goals, and their self-discipline. Dealing with a tonal language or a language with a different script, the student need make some big decisions about how they want to learn, and how much. Relatively speaking, Filipino/Pilipino/Tagalog is easy.

I learned Spanish as an adult. I am now fluent at a professional/business level. About 10-15% of Tagalog is Spanish, and the spelling of Tagalog words are all based on Spanish sounds.

I learned to read Thai. I can write some, but my vocabulary is very small. 90% of my Thai came from taking private one-on-one classes while living in Thailand for 6 months.

I studied some Tagalog, some Korean, and some Thai using Rosetta Stone.

If you just want to learn some Tagalog to get around as a tourist, enough people speak excellent English in the Philippines you will probably never be able to use it. The Filipinos who don't speak English will typically avoid speaking to you, even when you try to speak Tagalog. Regardless, an immersion product, like Rosetta Stone, is probably not as useful because much of the vocabulary and context is not related to what you will want to know (do you really need to say the boy is under the soccer ball?).

If you want to seriously learn the language to be able to carry on casual or business conversations, commit early and realize there is far more work involved. To really practice Tagalog, you will need to go to less savory parts of Manila, or plan on getting outside of Manila, Cebu, away from the red light districts in Olongapo and Angeles, and avoid the resort areas like Puerta Galera and Boracay. To really use Tagalog, you need to go to areas where those who don't speak English are willing to make an effort to understand you.

For me, I first needed to learn the alphabet. Since spelling is based on Spanish phonetics and the Roman alphabet, this was easy for me with Tagalog. For other languages, like Thai, you CANNOT consistently pronounce Thai correctly using Romanized phonetics. T one rules are only consistent in Thai script. Among other challenges, the Romanization is wildly inconsistent. You learn it one way, and then another source using different phonetics mires you in confusion. The same is probably also true of Korean, as it is also a phonetic language. Learning Chinese will likely be different. This part of Tagalog is easy though.

Second, I realized for me, I need to take notes. As adults we want to take notes to help remember key points. If you take the notes in English, you are handicapping yourself. This is more difficult, and far more important, in languages with their own script.

Third, again for me, I knew learning translation would create a permanent handicap. Early on, translation is easier, later on translation must be unlearned as it stilts actual conversation and thinking. You just can't translate fast enough. Even now, being fluent in Spanish, translating gives me a headache and frustrates me. I either have a conversation in Spanish, thinking in Spanish, or I have a conversation in English thinking in English. If I know a word in one language and not the other, my whole train of thought is derailed. Avoiding learning translation is where Rosetta Stone shines.

I like the idea of Rosetta Stone. If you are disciplined enough to do the lessons regularly, you will expand your spoken vocabulary rapidly. You will remember what you learn. For reading and writing, Rosetta Stone is limited. I doubt it will do much for reading and writing with non-Roman scripts. Like any learning tool, disciplined study will yield results.

Rosetta Stone is very expensive. Competing products like L-Lingo or products using different methods like Pimsleur, TellMeMore.com, Assimil, or Fluenz (supposedly the best, but only in a few languages) are a fraction of the cost of Rosetta Stone. Many of the different methods will work better for some people than others. Assimil is translation based. Pimsleur is hard to describe, but has a very good fluency success rate (supposedly). Look up Fluenz also, as the method and reviews suggest it is very effective in the few languages they offer.

Besides cost, what is the other drawback to Rosetta Stone? The drawbacks are legion.

Version 2 is good. Version 2 is how Rosetta Stone grew into a powerhouse. The voice recognition is very primitive. Version 3 is a refinement of version 2 with improved continuity, a smoother interface, better quizzes, and the ability to get rid of the stupid \\"must have CD with you at all times\\" limitation. You can also advance or return to the exact spot where you left off earlier.

Unfortunately, Rosetta Stone dropped support for Version 2. Even though they were selling version 2 from their own website in 2012, they dropped support. Mac users are especially impacted as Mac OSX Lion will no longer run PPC apps, and Rosetta Stone never ported Version 2 to Intel. So, if you bought Version 2 in 2012 to use on a Mac, you were ripped off by Rosetta Stone. Join the crowd.

Windows users should not be too smug about the situation, as the end of Version 2 support means your product will have all sorts of issues too, unless you downgrade to WinXP.

Version 3 runs on current platforms, and is supported (to the extent Rosetta Stone supports any product). Version 3 is easily the pinnacle of the Rosetta Stone application. Given so many users prefer version 3 to version 4 though, don't be surprised if they pull a Microsoft and force users to their new product nobody wants.

Total 4e, is a disappointing retrograde of Rosetta Stone. To be fair, if you are always connected -- literally 100% of the time, never a lost packet -- and live your life via social media, Total 4e might work for you. Don't expect to use the highly touted iOS apps on your iPhone or iPad though unless you are connected 100% of the time with those devices also. The whole idea of quickly practicing while in line or waiting in an office...yeah, that doesn't conform to the Rosetta Stone licensing model.

Speaking of which, Rosetta Stone now has two components and two licensing models. There is the software application and the online social media part. The application can be run as long as they support it on current platforms. The online social media component is now on a subscription basis. You pay for every month in which you want to participate. You can still use the app on your computer, but you just paid a premium for online access you aren't using unless you continue to pay the subscription.

Given there are many free or lower cost websites where learners can interact and practice language skills, why pay Rosetta Stone a monthly premium for less content? Therein lies the reason so many people look at Total 4e and then try to find version 3 before supplies run out.

How about another suggestion?

Try L-Lingo. L-Lingo uses a very similar learning model to Rosetta Stone. The interface actually has more features than Rosetta Stone and you can customize the interface to use Roman phonetics or native script. They have iPad and iPhone/IPod Touch iOS apps which you can use on a plane, or anywhere else, with or without Internet access. Best of all, all of their programs together (Win or Mac desktop, iPad, iPhone/iPod Touch) are less than half the cost of Rosetta Stone Level I.

L-Lingo specializes in Asian languages. They are probably a superior option to Rosetta Stone Total 4e for most users. L-Lingo offers a free trial for their desktop application, and also for their iOS applicastions for some languages.

There are other good options listed above, particularly Fluenz and Pimsleur which use different methods. I own Powerdvd 11 ultra but I just want to warn potential purchasers what they could be letting themselves in for. Whether you intend to pick this up from Amazon or from Cyberlink themselves, be aware that from version 12 onwards Cyberlink has included the horror which is called Cinavia. This is basically protection against pirated movies and sits within the audio track. Many movies at the cinema now contain this and anyone smuggling a camcorder into there local cinema will find it can effect them too. After approx 20 mins the audio will mute and a message will appear telling them what has happened. When used with PowerDVD 12 or 13, this does effect original purchased movies as well, but only if they are using programs such as Anydvd-HD which is used to make your pc region free as well as cope with the latest movie protection etc. It is Anydvd-HD which is falsely alerting the protection, not the movie. If you have no intention of using Anydvd-HD then it doesn't really effect you, though it's worth saying that there is a feature within it to circumvent Cinavia, but is just a work around and does not remove the protection all together. Some original blu-ray 3D movies I own clearly label 'Cinavia' at the bottom of the case on the rear side. Not all do but movies like 'Hotel Translyvania' is one such title. Also note that the PS3 has Cinavia in-built as well. For me I am staying with Powerdvd 11 for this exact reason. Oh, and some other players such as TMT6 also contain this protection. Better to check first before parting with your hard earned ca$h. Plenty of information online about Cinavia (you can check Powerdvd and Anydvd forums etc). Hope this helps you!

For about $40 you get excellent OCR software. It does excellent recognition of fairly complicated documents (2 column docs in fairly poor image resolution).

However its interface to scanner is so deficient, that you will likely have to resort to other software to scan paper documents. Here are the problems in build 12.0.104.167; Part #1132.25:

1. Scanning Letter pages (8.5" x 11") from automatic document feeder, results in oversized PDF pages (8.53" x 11.72" or even Legal size). Using other scan software via native TWAIN interface creates correctly sized documents.

2. Scanned/recognized pages are often reordered (20 pages ADF scan on 4 CPU PC); sometimes a page is duplicated. When OCR an already scanned document, no reordering occurs.

3. Scanner interface does not allow selection of paper size, nor the scanner interface allows access native dialog of the TWAIN driver.

4. There is no function to crop oversized pages.

5. Technical support while responsive, could not reproduce any of the errors, but suggested buying FineReader 12.

Summary: It is good to have as a backup solution for OCR of complex documents, when your primary PDF editor (e.g. PhantomPDF) does not provide adequate OCR, but not very useful as the primary application for digitizing paper documents.

It is sad that an excellent OCR backend is buried by failure to provide a simple and robust interface to a scanner.

I have used Mac TurboTax (and its predecessor MacInTax) for over 20 years. Finally, I have been forced to abandon TurboTax completely on account of Intuit's evolving design philosophy to wrest ultimate control of your tax return away from you and force it to look the way they want it to look.

Specifically, my complaint is that TurboTax is increasingly limiting the user's ability to OVERRIDE values on the return. In the past -- for many, many years -- a user could override any calculated or transferred value anywhere on the return. But beginning in 2011 and continuing to the present, that ability has become increasingly restricted. As a practical meter, this means that you can't necessarily make your tax return look the way YOU want it to look. Now, Intuit essentially tells you how it HAS to look (if you use their software).

At first, limitations on overrides only appeared on Form 8582 (Passive Activities) AND its worksheets. In 2011, 2012, and 2013 I had to prepare Form 8582 and its worksheets with a TYPEWRITER (!!!). But then in 2013, it got even worse when the "no overrides" principle was extended to Form 4562 (Depreciation). My federal return makes extensive use of both Form 8582 and Form 4562. These are critical forms and without the ability to complete them the way I want to complete them, I simply can't and won't use the TurboTax program. So I'm done with it.

What to do now? In 2013, as an experiment, I purchased and used both TurboTax and H&R Block's Tax Software to prepare my return. Interestingly, the paper return I ended up filing (I always file paper returns) was a mixture of pages from the two programs. The difference between the two programs was huge. H&R Block is what TurboTax used to be: It is intuitive, easy to use, and every entry on every form is totally within control of the user. You can prepare your return to look EXACTLY like you want want it to look -- H&R Block is not looking over your shoulder, so tospeak, while you do it. It's also much cheaper, at $35 for the "Deluxe" Federal and State version.

I will admit that TurboTax is slicker, has a fancier interface, and might cover some unusual tax situations that H&R Block doesn't. (But not in my return, which is pretty complicated as these things go.) But I don't need "slick." I need something that will prepare my return the way I want it prepared.... exactly as I want it prepared. If you are an experienced DIY tax return preparer with even a moderately complicated return, you should want the same thing. I would highly recommend anyone to investigate the H&R Block product. For me, it's perfect.

My wife and I have been using Quicken almost daily for more than 15 years. As I said in the January update the budget module in the 2014 version is very difficult to use. I find that the only way I can do what I want to is to have a pen and paper next to me, and a calculator on screen. The problem is trying to manage budgets month to month.

I can't use the method designed into the program because it is an annual method (Details layout). If we overspend one month and look all the way to the right what I see is the amount over or under budget, which I already knew. That is of no help to me.

Lets say we budget $100/mo which is $1,200/year. If we under-spend in January by $10 I want to change the January budget to $90 and make February $110. As soon as I set the January budget amount to 90 the column all the way to the right tells me I'm on budget and showing a $0 balance - which I am momentarily - but I've lost the amount that I'm wanting to move to February. All I have in the balance column is $0. Useless.

What I had in the 2011 version was the yearly budget amount, in this case $1,200. When I changed January to $90 the total budget amount would change to $1,190. That told me I had $10 more to add to Feb. I've lost that data. Hence the pencil and paper. It's no small thing because we have about 50 categories and the way Quicken budgeting is designed my time doubles to use the budgeting.

In the 2014 design I have to scroll right to see the \\"Balance\\" as it is hidden unless I have a wide enough screen. In the 2011 version I could have two windows open, one with the budget and one with the actuals. I could see all of the columns I wanted to. That isn't possible in the 2014 budget.

Budgeting is why we bought the program - and it's broken (in my opinion) in the 2014 version. The 2011 version was MUCH better.

If Intuit would simply add a column showing the total budgeted amount they can keep the balance column and I'd be happy. Also I'd want the Budgeted amount locked on the screen so it didn't scroll with the months. I always want to see that right most column.

Scrolling is another area that is a mess in 2014. In the Details budget view if I'm looking at the November data it will often scroll back to January when I operate the scroll bar or the mouse wheel. Honestly I don't know what the formula is to make that happen because it doesn't happen all of the time. But it certainly is annoying because I think I'm entering a number in November but end up in some other month.

I am so frustrated because we use perhaps 45% of Quickens total feature set, but the important ones that we use are a mess.

I've used TurboTax for the last two years, including this one. Last year, I was able to use Deluxe and my situation has not changed, so I bought that product. Behold, even though the forms list includes Schedule C for self-employment, the program would not properly handle the entries. I ended up having to upgrade to the Premier version. Strike one.
With the upgraded version installed (Windows), I continued my tax prep. Unfortunately, entries I had made related to the business in the limited Deluxe version were now blocked out in the forms mode of the Premier version. I could not change the entries, except by making them 0 in the interview mode. In other words, entries in interview mode prevented editing in forms mode. Strike two.
In general, I find the interface in TurboTax to be cumbersome and inflexible. While I appreciate the completeness of the program and was forced to use it over the products of your competitors, I find other tax prep software easier to use. Here are some major issues:

The program is fine if you want to go through the entire interview, although the organization and presentation of topics in the interview are cumbersome. It is not easy to view interview entries directly in the form--you have to change to forms mode and open the form, then change back to interview if you want to continue. This is in contrast to HR Block's product.

The forms mode includes many "smart worksheets," which are used to enter and/or calculate detailed information. They are helpful when navigating through the forms while entering information, but are cumbersome when reviewing the forms. There is no way to hide these worksheets. Work-around: print or preview the form to PDF and review it in your PDF viewer. Cumbersome.

It is sometimes difficult to find a particular interview topic. There is a topics list, but no search function in that list. There is a search box on the main page, but a search there will bring up forum discussions. I wanted to determine whether or not I had to do estimated taxes and had to do a Google search outside of the program to find out how to get there (type 1040-ES in the search box).

I needed to make a Safe Harbor Election for Small Business. It turns out that TT can print this form, but it is nearly impossible to find it. In fact, it is hidden in the new rental interview topic, and can't even be found when going through the interview a second time. TurboTax phone help was clueless on this one, as well. It is not at all accessible form the Forms mode.

In forms view, only forms currently being used show up in the tree. I could not find the rather ubiquitous Schedule A and had to search for it. There is not an option to show all (or most common) forms in the tree, rather than just the ones in your return.

On the positive side, TurboTax is much more complete when it comes to Publicly Traded Partnerships and K-1 entries than any other program I have found. In fact, I was forced to use TT for this capability.

Complaining is easy to do, so in order to provide you with as objective a review as possible, I'm going to start with what I like about this software. I love Quicken. I've been using it since 2006 and my father (who introduced me to the product) has been using it for decades. What Quicken has always lacked is a substantial budgeting component. That issue is finally addressed in 2013 and it works reasonably well! However, those who added this feature likely aren't that familiar with personal budgeting themselves, as the system they set up is clunky at best and not very intuitive. However, we have gotten it to work for ourselves and our budget and now we couldn't be happier!

The real shame with this product is its mobile app. Finally releasing a mobile version of Quicken was what convinced me to upgrade to 2013 from 2012. Given the complex record-keeping that Quicken itself does, an app that is simply a companion to the desktop version (instead of a replacement) is understandable, especially when one considers Intuit's ownership of Mint.com. However, what is not understandable is why Quicken released this mobile app with such little development. It looks pretty, but has failed in two different ways for me since purchasing 2013 (two weeks ago!). I understand that bugs can occur in commercial software, but for me as an individual user to experience two separate bugs in the syncing and mobile features in two weeks is unacceptable. The most unfortunate part is Quicken's technical support staff, who are either utterly unhelpful (perhaps due to a lack of experience with the software themselves) or condescending. The online forum staff are more knowledgable, but it seems like they themselves are kept in the dark often on the inner workings of the online components of Quicken.

All in all, this is a great product but unfortunately the new features have a steep learning curve for the average user. If any computer software reviewer sites out there are reading this, here is my suggestion: Publish a step-by-step guide for how to budget in Quicken. Include checking to make sure the budget is zero-sum and how to use Savings Goals in tandem with the budget itself.

One last warning to fellow users: it appears that the budgets are saved in the Quicken Cloud, NOT your desktop. That means that, should something go wrong with your online account that requires its deletion and re-creation, you will find that your budget has disappeared. Make sure you record your final budget in a second form (i.e. a spreadsheet) to make sure that you don't lose that info if the unfortunate were to occur!

My wife is a native Telugu speaker. I purchased Instant Immersion Telugu Level 1 to help me (a native English speaker) learn her mother tongue. After I downloaded the program, my wife and I went through a few of the vocabulary lists together. It only took a few minutes for me to realize I'd thrown $30 out the window - every few words or phrases my wife would either get a confused look on her face or burst out laughing. Many of the translations, it turns out, are wrong, and some are simply absurd. Examples -    - \\"Left\\" and \\"right\\" are presented together in the course, obviously connoting the relative directions, as in \\"left turn\\" and \\"right turn.\\" However, the Telugu word presented as the translation of \\"left\\" means \\"to leave\\" or \\"let go\\" and has nothing to do with the direction \\"left.\\" Similarly, the word presented as the Telugu equivalent of \\"right\\" only means \\"right\\" in the sense of \\"correct\\"; the Telugu word for the direction \\"right\\" is something completely different than what's presented here.    - Instant Immersion's Telugu translation for \\"Cheers!\\" is an artificial construction for a term that doesn't exist in Telugu. Literally, the Telugu that's presented translates back into English as something to the effect of \\"Let us touch cups together,\\" which my wife assures me sounds even more absurd in Telugu than it does in English.    - Instant Immersion's Telugu translation for \\"Thank you\\" means \\"salutations\\" and not \\"thanks.\\" According to my wife, no one speaking any dialect of Telugu would use Instant Immersion's term to express thanks.    The above are just a sample of the problems we came across in this software. Though we didn't go through the entire course, it seems likely, if not probable, that it's riddled with hundreds of issues like these.    Instant Immersion's Telugu Level 1 seems to have been produced with little concern for accuracy and appears to rely on the translations of native Telugu speakers who did not understand English well enough to know what words they were being asked to say.    A disappointing purchase, to say the least.

I've used MS Office for years on PC's. I don't need Powerpoint or Outlook and I was unhappy to pay a higher price for a single computer license. In previous years, Word and Excel previously came in a three license version for home users.

I was disappointed in how different the UI was compared to Office 2010. I'm still looking for the features I've come very used to. They are in there, I just have to look for them. Changing the page size, working with styles, and the other options are just slightly different. One difference I especially dislike. That is the track changes feature. I'm used to the changes showing up inside the doc with deleted words crossed out and inserted words in the editors color. In this version all changes in the document are no longer visible but noted in balloon notes to the right side. I find this much more difficult to use, especially on Mac screens where the fonts are especially small. OpenOffice on the other hand has balloon text that you can actually read. Another difference that I'm still trying to get used to is the find/replace/heading list pane on the left of the document. The find/replace option is gone and put into the upper right of the screen. I've also discovered a few quirks in the headings listing where they don't show unless I move the slider up and down. I can't figure that one out.

So, I'm a bit peeved at the changes that need not have been made in the user interface, but since I must use MS Word for my writing, I'll just have to figure it out.

One other major gripe I have about this version is the inclusion of a trial of Outlook. Outlook has been the favorite attack mechanism for virus writers for years. Since I no longer work in an office, Outlook has no value to me. I use web based email readers. The problem is that since I'm using a smaller solid state disk drive, I find no reason to keep extra software on my machine that I'll never use or pay for. Outlook can not be deleted by the averageuser. You have to get into a UNIX shell, navigate to the Outlook directory and delete it that way. I won't recommend that to anyone, since you need sudo root access and I would never encourage a novice user to get in with that level of access who could potentially screw up other system necessities.

I wonder if MS is trying to discourage Mac users from using their products. But if you need advanced formatting features, track changes, and industry output options, this is pretty much the only game in town. If you don't need all that, go with Pages. It's a lot cheaper and has most necessities that the average user needs.
