Update 11/10/2016: -------------------------------------  I am updating my review to reflect changes in the Creative Cloud Products.  I use Windows 10 Pro 64 bit, so finding good 3rd party commercial software for web design has been a challenge as most are designed for the Mac.   Creative Cloud is primarily a professional's suite of software. If you are not intending to use the products for work or freelance then I would suggest avoiding Adobe's Creative Cloud unless you have the funds to spare. If you are or have used their software I highly recommend exporting in standards output such as css, html, png, svg  eg... and compatible versions of PDF and PSD files. This way if you lose access or can't load Adobe's software you can still load the work files into another application.  The proprietary file complaint is valid but if you export into common file formats you will not lose any work.  As of the end of 2016 Adobe has revamped their entire suite of offerings. They have eliminated entirely the useful web design software "Edge" projects and cut back and streamlined Dreamweaver and their other design apps.  This puts these in-line with many open source software and offerings from other companies that either do not have a subscription model or a choice between one off purchase with upgrade offers as new version are available OR an subscription model which you choose which you prefer.  Due to the changes in the Adobe line of products I personally have found better options elsewhere for most of the web and graphic design work I do.  There are options now that were not available earlier in 2016 and previous for windows based software so if you do not want to be tied to Adobe's Subscription model you no longer need to choose this company.  I have set my subscription to not renew and will see how that goes when my subscription ends, others have complained of cancellation not going through.  For the vast majority of the current adobe products, now at the end of 2016, there are better and more powerful options available such as from Affinity and Smith Micro as well as open source options including Brackets for coding web pages directly.   Hitfilm and Resolve are alternative video and special effects software with more bang for the buck and easier to use. These are alternatives and don't match up directly with adobe's software so don't look at it as better or worse just different but allowing to do similar things.  For me Creative Cloud is a set of tools and like any tool you will occasionally look around to see if there is something else better for the job at hand. I have discovered better options that are easier and do more and support is easier to deal with especially when they actually know the products which Adobe's support do not. Hard to answer questions or solve issues when they don't even know how the software works.  I like the Creative Cloud but like I said the software has recently changed and been cut back to the point I can do exactly the same thing with strictly open source software now and 3rd Party software that is the cost of less than one months fee or 3 months worth of CC subscription.  Not worth it for me any longer.  I may look back in the future to the Adobe's product line but for now I am moving on as the software really has become just like anything else out there. Nothing special here anymore.  Tip:  Pay attention to the subscription version for the price you have chosen. Lower price tends to be locked to a 12 month contract.  No such thing as one time only for lower price with Adobe at least not in 2016.  ------------------------------------------------ Original Review - ( 2014 ) ------------------------------------------------  I have been a subscriber to Adobe's Creative Cloud since it started.  During that time they have consistently updated the software and come out with 4 or 5 new software only offered through the subscription service.  Not all the updates were that great but bug fixes and some ofof the new features added have been useful.  Comparing Creative Cloud version of some of the titles in CS6 the changes for example in Flash Pro have been a down grade in some respects.  Photoshop has had a few features added that are nice but for the most part the CS6 version works well as is.  The Creative Cloud only apps like Muse are nice if you want to put together an html based site pretty quickly.  Basically everything in the Masters Collection and then some is what you get with the monthly or annual subscription, instead of $2500 you pay $600 per year and they do update the software pretty regularly so for the updates and bug fixes it is worth it.  A lot of people don't like the subscription service and complain that the new features added and bug fixes are not worth the ongoing expense of this service and prefer the one time payment of CS6.  I can't see anything wrong with that.  If you are only going to be using one or two software and not really use much more of the offerings than that, then I would say this would be a waste of money for you.  If you are going to be using Photoshop, Dreamweaver, Acrobat and 3 or 4 more of the applications then it may be worth it for you.  For me I create websites, do youtube video's and create video and audio products the entire creative cloud is very nice.  If you aren't going to be using the software on a regular basis then $600 a year may not be worth it to you.  It is sort of a forced situation where if you sign up you have two choices, pay month to month without a contract for $80 a month or go with a annual contract for $50 a month.  There are first year discounts for various pre-creative cloud product owners and students but those end after the first year and then regular price is $50 a month.  Students may get a special price on going as long as they are enrolled in school but as I am not a student I don't know for sure what those prices are.  You can install applications on as many computers as you want but you can only have two computers activated at one time.  You just signout of creative cloud desktop on a computer and then sign in on another one to begin using the software if you have gone beyond the two activations.  It isn't that big of a deal, unless you need to have them running at the sametime then you won't be allowed to.  You can ask for more activations but no guarantee they will add more for you but it has happened for some.  Once a month the activation software will run and verify you have an active subscription, this requires an internet connection.  Sometimes this happens more than once a month and it can lock you out of the software until it does verify.  Sometimes your login details can be lost from the creative cloud desktop which forces you to retype your adobe id email and password for your Adobe account. This is annoying and has happened to me several times a day for days then it stops asking me and just stays logged in, seems to be an intermittent problem.  Every so often individual apps will ask to be registered, is not suppose to happen but it does.  Isn't a big deal, just click a button and it does it but it can be annoying. Also requires an active internet connection.  Support is horrible, I can't understand phone support and they keep repeating what I say and end up just randomly picking a problem out of their scripts to define the problem I am having. Is not useful and wastes a lot of time.  After the Adobe break in my credit card was canceled which forced me to contact Adobe and they gave me two months credit to give me time to get a new card and to I guess appease me for my trouble.  The problem is you only get a maximum of two months of credit from Adobe and after that they won't issue any more.  I ended up buying a new subscription from Amazon because I was not going to give my new card to Adobe and they canceled my original subscription.  The problem here is that you can't use an account that already has an Adobe Creative Cloud subscriptionso I had to use another account or create a new one.  I ended up doing that and then contacting Adobe and they canceled my subscription through them.  This leaves me with two Adobe accounts but now Amazon is handling the payment charges and not Adobe, I am happy about that but not having two accounts at Adobe.  If you choose to do the samething, switch from Adobe charging your credit card to Amazon charging your credit card then you have to create or use a different Adobe account and pay Amazon first, then have Adobe cancel your first subscription.  They ask for  a 24 character redemption code to verify but Amazon subscription does not use them so you have to verify with the person some other way.  Phone support just does not understand this and won't do anything to help you from my experience, chat support is a little better and that is how I got this resolved.  I do use Adobe's software on a regular basis so for me having access to all their software for $600 a year is worth it, for others it may not be.  If you are a hobbyist or someone that doesn't use the software that much then it probably like I said above is not something you want to get involved with.  If you cancel while under the annual contract then you pay 50% of the remaining balance for the year whether you use it or not.  Just walk into this wide eyed and know exactly what you are getting into and what you will be using the software for.  I am happy with the software and for me it is worth it. I like having the software updated and new features and new software added but sometimes things aren't all that great and the beta software like  Edge Reflow or their new WYSWYG Website software Muse is buggy until they come out with the next version or bug updates, sometimes even then the issues stick around.  Eventually they fix it but it can take awhile, some issues though are just their by design because the designers have their way of doing things and you have yours, the designers win out no matter the number of complaints and feature requests.  The beta programs are interesting to participate in, I do it as little as possible if I can help it.  Overall I like the Creative Cloud and I find it economical versus paying $2500 for masters collection of CS6.  Many don't agree which is fine, it all depends on what and how you use the applications.  I have gone a month or two without even opening one and then all of a sudden I am consistently using 5 or 6 with 3 or 4 being used simultaneously.  Some of the software like Premiere and After Effects I just can't get into so I purchased 3rd Party software for half the price of the stand alone and am consistently using Photoshop, Audition and several other software to help create what I create.  Though it is nice to know After Effects and Premiere are there if I want to learn them, I don't live in Adobe software I just use the tools that work and 70% of the software I use is Adobe so $50 a month is worth it for that.  Turn the autorenewal off if you can and decide at the annual renewal date if it is worth it to continue or not. I just can't find any real alternatives to the software I use regularly or I would probably switch from CC as well.  I do use Open Source and paid 3rd Party Software I just keep returning to Adobe's because it is easier to do things or impossible to do in alternate software.  The haters and complainers talking people away from the subscription some of their points are valid some are just personal biases or vindictiveness over Adobe as a company.  I am not a personal fan of Adobe myself but in my world the software is just a tool, these tools are really good and though some don't work how I prefer them to they do get the job done.  As long as you go into these subscriptions with eyes open and know exactly what to expect then weigh your uses with the price and see if it is worth it to you. You can just pay month to month without having any contract but you pay additional for that privilege, if you only need it for a project or two that maybe the better way to go for you.

--It's also illegal to sell OEM software.

I have no way of knowing how this OEM software got into the batch that Amazon is selling. I only know that's what I was sold.

Intuit likens itself to the Apple of the tax software industry. This assumes that Product Leadership trumps Customer Service, but in a mature market that's a false perception. I have a myriad programs I use for art: Manga Studio, Photoshop, Corel Painter, Illustrator, etc. Sketchbook Pro is the one I like to turn to when I want to focus on my drawing and NOT on a "program". With an uncluttered interface and plenty of terrific tools that mimic real life media, Sketchbook Pro is the closest thing to drawing on a real piece of paper. It's also the EASIEST drawing software to jump right into with very little learning curve. Most of the tools are self-explanatory and there are just a few new features that might take a bit of extra exploration to figure out like the new perspective guides and the new layer states that mimic some Photoshop capabilities.

Sketchbook Pro is chock full of drawing tools. You get to play with pencils, airbrush, markers, pens, paint, charcoal, textures, shapes, splatters and smudge brushes.

The area where it really shines (for me anyway) is the Copic marker set. You get 6 different Copic markers that mimic their real life counterparts: a multi-liner, drawing marker, super brush nib, fine nib, medium broad nib and an extra broad nib. Then, to top it off you have a color palette that features a huge library of real Copic colors along with their letter/number designations and names. It looks like the Copic markers caps arranged nicely in rows. Need to use "Cherry White"? It's right there. Want to use Y32 Cashmere? You got it. Click on the palette's upper rainbow of squares and each "drawer" of marker colors is immediately accessible. It's organized via color family. You have all of your blues together, all of the reds, grays, etc. To top it all off, this new version of Sketchbook has a colorless blender that WORKS LIKE THE REAL THING!!!

Copic markers cost an arm and a leg. At set of 12 colors is 95.88, not to mention the additional cost for the various nibs. Here they are in Sketchbook Pro and they work just like the real ones only they won't break the bank. Get yourself a Wacom stylus in hand and color away, just like you are sitting there with your basket of markers and a sketch book! For $65! Think of the hundreds of dollars worth of savings. ;-)

Of course the other tools in Sketchbook Pro are just as awesome. Besides the great set of tools, you have the option to customize brushes and create your own. There are also sets of brushes you can download for free. Just google "sketchbook pro brushes download" and get some goodies like cross hatching brushes, hair brushes and more.

One area where Sketchbook Pro totally outdoes Photoshop and even Painter: blending brushes. Sketchbook Pro has blending down to an art. It has the most wonderful, glorious, natural feeling smudge brushes ever. Trying to blend something in Photoshop is a time consuming pain in the...In PS there are all sorts of fancy techniques and if you try to use the blend tool, be prepared to sit around and wait for your cursor to catch up. The only other program I have that has this type of blending ability is Manga Studio, but even that program has a different feel to its blending brushes. Sketchbook Pro gets it right.

Other nifty features:

*Super easy transformation - just click the button and start dragging the handles on your drawing to adjust
*French curves and ellipse guides to help guide your drawing, just like the real tools
*Perspective guides - turn these on and they will constrain your drawing so that it's in the perspective you choose. An amazing time saver, especially if you want to draw buildings and the like
*Symmetry - Want to draw something symmetrical? These guides will copy your drawing horizontally, vertically or both at the same time
*Steady stroke - This is a feature I love in Manga Studio. Sketchbook Pro has added it as well and you can dial it up, down or turn it off completely. It really helps smooth out the jitters and wobbles in your drawing for a professional and polished look
*Draw styles - If you want to quickly draw a shape, just use the preset shapes and drag them to however you want them to look, let go of your cursor and the shape will draw in whatever pen or brush you are using.
*Layers - You can now group layers and apply layer adjustments like darken, multiply and so on (Photoshop style)
*Handy pucks - use one puck to instantly change your brush size by dragging one way or the other over it. Use the other to instantly change the color of your ink/paint or the saturation &/or luminance (you can also use it to capture a color on your canvas)
*Improved selection ability - Sketchbook Pro 7 has added a bunch of new selection tools
*New flipbook - a handy new tool for animators

I've used Sketchbook Pro with a Cintiq and also with a Wacom tablet. It works flawlessly with both and all of the drawing tools are pressure sensitive. You can set the stylus responsiveness via a slider box that you can get by going to edit at the top of the screen.

The thing about Sketchbook Pro is that is has a lot of capabilities but none of these ever get in the way of your drawing or painting. That's the lovely thing about this program is that it's a digital sketchbook first and foremost and a "program" second. It's designed to be EASY to use so you can start drawing and painting right away without having to learn a complicated software program. Seriously, your grandma or your 3 year old could figure out the basics of this program. Click on the thing that looks like a pencil: draw. Click on the thing that looks like an eraser: erase. Click on the thing that looks like a marker: color. EASY! Just jump right in and start DRAWING instead of learning & figuring things out.

However, if you want some of the "extras" they are there (for the more advanced user) but they aren't cluttering up the interface and intimidating or distracting you from your drawing. Even the more advanced tools are very intuitive - more so than any program I've ever "played" with. ;-)

Another quick note: Sketchbook Pro has never lagged on me. It's blazing fast and feels just like I'm using real tools instead of drawing and then waiting for the cursor to catch up as it sometimes does in Photoshop or Painter.

I really love Sketchbook Pro for when I want to just draw. It's like a digital toybox with everything I need to sketch, doodle, draw & paint where it feels like I'm just sitting down with my sketchbook instead of sitting down at the computer. I highly recommend it for anyone who is interested in digital drawing & painting and wants a "natural" feel instead of wrestling with having to learn a complicated software program. Or, for those of you who already have Photoshop, Painter and so on, it's a great tool to have in your arsenal of art programs, especially when you want a more free and realistic feeling (or just have a love for Copic markers and want the holy grail of Copic marker goodness oozing from your drawing program, lol).

All-in-all I highly recommend it. At $65 it's inexpensive enough to add to your pile of drawing toys. It would also make a great gift if you are looking for some drawing software to give to a family member who loves art and wants to explore digital drawing/painting. Just make sure your artist has a tablet with a stylus to draw on to compliment the program. I recommend a [[ASIN:B00EN27U9U Wacom Intuos Pen and Touch Small Tablet]]. It's the least expensive Wacom option for someone just starting out (Wacom is the brand most professionals use). Or you can go with a [[ASIN:B008Y40DQU Turcom TS-6580B 8" x 5" Graphic Drawing Capture Pen and Touch Tablet - Black]] for half the price (less quality = less price).

Note: If you have an earlier version, you may be wondering if Sketchbook Pro 7 is worth the upgrade. If you are into the whole Copic markers thing, you might like the fact that colors are now labeled just like the real marker caps and the fact that you have a colorless blender designed to work like the real thing. The new perspective guides are also a help to some types of drawing. I also found that many of the brushes, even though the "same" as before design wise, work a bit better, smoother, faster. For me, the new animation tools are a waste - something I'll never use. I do really appreciate the new transform, flood fill and selection tools though as well as the new layer capabilities. If you have the $ you'll probably think the new tools are worth it as they make it so you can do more work in Sketchbook Pro itself without having to buzz over to Photoshop or another program for techy type things.

Also, this is the PC / Mac version of this program. There is a mobile / tablet app that is available as well that you can get directly from Autodesk or via Google Play or your iPad, etc.

I'm a man of simple needs when it comes to image editing, I need only a few key features and I'm happy using whatever app is available. Knowing this, I decided that I don't really need the full power of photoshop as the pricing of that App is overkill for what I use it for (I've owned photoshop back in the 7, CS, CS2 days) and then I set off in search of an App that will meet my needs...

As I said, my needs are simple and there are only Six features that matter to me.

1. Pricing
2. RAW Conversion, the app has to support RAW file formats for my camera!
3. Deconvolution Filter or Smart Sharpening
4. Color Management
5. Calculations / Arithmetic Tool
6. Decent Plug-In Support

The contenders for my search were GIMP, Photoshop Elements 11, Paint Shop Pro X5 Ultimate, and Photoshop.

PRICING

So, to start my budget is upto $100 and that right there means that the full version of Photoshop is automatically eliminated. I don't do this professionally and in this economy, I cannot afford to spend $30 (Subscription pricing, the crook that keeps on robbing) a month or $600 for just one application.

GIMP is free so, that's a fairly good feature to have!
Photoshop Elements 11 is anywhere from $70 to $100 so that's safe.
Paint Shop Pro X5 Ultimate ranges from $55 to $70 so that's safe as well.
The advantage here goes to GIMP with Photoshop CS 6 being completely eliminated.

GIMP = 5
PSP = 4
PSE = 3
CS6 = 1

RAW CONVERSION

GIMP has no built in functions for RAW Conversion but, there are plug-ins available for it so, by default you cannot just load up a RAW file but, I won't eliminate it because it does have the support.

Photoshop would obviously be king of this area but, pricing has eliminated it.

Photoshop Elements has the second most feature rich RAW Image Editor with only a few tools removed from the CS6Plug-in.

Paint Shop Pro X5 has a basic plug-in that will convert the images but, don't expect shadow / highlight, curves, lens correction, or any majorly advanced settings in this app because they don't exist.

I'll be honest, this is on my list but, given the fact that RAW Therapee is free and my Olympus MFT has a decent RAW Image Editor, it is probably the only area where I would be willing to sacrifice if I had to.

With all that said, Photoshop is king and its little sibling clearly beats out the others with PSP X5 Ultimate coming in last.

CS6 = 5
PSE = 5
PSP = 3
GIMP = 3

DECONVOLUTION FILTER / SMART SHARPENING

Honestly, this is a big tool to be missing! This tool allows you to remove lens blur and sharpen the image in such a way that will not create the Halo effect of a tool like USM. Straight off the bat, GIMP and PSP X5 Ultimate get whacked for not featuring this.

Photoshop is again king here, the tools is straight forward

Photoshop Elements has the same tool so, this is equally as impressive.

GIMP has a bastardized version of smart sharpening available via plug-in but, nothing builtin to the app.

PSP 11 Ultimate, no such option built into the app but, it does support the leading Smart Sharpening Plug-in in Focalblade. However, this will cost you $60 so, now we've pushed the cost to $115 just to get this feature.

CS6 = 5
PSE = 5
PSP = 3
GIMP = 1

COLOR MANAGEMENT

Each of these apps supports color management to some degree. The more color space options you have the better but, not everyone is going to have to work in LAB or even CMYK (I like to work in CMYK sometimes and having LAB minimizes color clipping when going from space to space) so, this might not be huge for some.

Photoshop simply has the best support across the board.

GIMP has decent support and worksvery similar to PSP X5 Ultimate.

PSP works a lot like GIMP and supports CMYK, HSL, and RGB.

Photoshop Elements is the worst of the bunch with support for only RGB and HSV.

CS6 = 5
PSP = 4
GIMP = 4
PSE = 2

CALCULATIONS / ARITHMETIC TOOL

This is one of the biggest tools I use because you cannot do professional quality Black and White Conversions without this tool! I would actually consider this a game changer as you cannot get this option via plug-in but, you can manually emulate it with the Channels tool.

Photoshop has the Calculations tool and it is hands down the most simple to use with great results.

PSP X5 Ultimate features the Arithmetic Tool and it is more flexible than the Calculations tool in CS6 but, you have to do the blending mode changes manually after the conversion has been completed. Still, this is a great tool and it works really well!

GIMP has no such tool but, you can use the Channels for the same function if you know what you're doing. This is not the easiest approach and honestly, it takes quite a bit of skill to pull off with the same quality as CS6 and PSP.

PS Elements has no such tool and no access to the Channels tool directly! To say that B&W Conversion is severely crippled in this app would be an understatement.

CS6 = 5
PSP = 5
GIMP = 3
PSE = 0

DECENT PLUGIN SUPPORT

This area is a bit of an anomaly because you have access to many of the same commercial plugins across 3 of the competitors and the fourth has a whole set of free plugins that you just don't have access to in the other 3.

CS6, PSE, and PSP all use the Adobe Plugin Engine and as long as care is taken for the development of the plugin, it will literally work across all 3 devices! This means, there's no real advantage to paying $600 for many plugins and that honestly hurts CS6 as far as value goes in mypersonal opinion.

GIMP cannot run any plugins from the group above but, there are a ton of free plugins available with varying degrees of quality, at the GIMP registry.

The one item that tips the scale here for me, is the fact that PSP X5 Ultimate comes bundled with FACEFILTER Studio 2 and NIK Color EFEX Pro 3 which would cost you close to $200 to include with PSE and CS6 (seriously, the NIK tools are professional grade all the way and some of the best in the business).

PSP = 5
CS6 = 4
PSE = 4
GIMP = 4

CONCLUSION

For me and the criteria I have, I found that PSP X5 Ultimate was a good cost / feature compromise and unfortunately, I will need to spend $60 to get the Deconvolution Filter but, I get about $200 worth of plugins to offset that and Corel has done a good Job with this app as I've really enjoyed using the trial version (I'll be making my purchase before my trial runs out).

And no, I'm not sayin this is as good as Photoshop at all! My score for CS 6 was clearly weighed down by the cost of the app and if you make money doing digital imaging then you will absolutely not find a better product than Photoshop period and it is not as close as these numbers indicate, they are weighted by my needs.

CS6 = 25
PSP = 24
PSE = 19
GIMP = 20

Take the following steps BEFORE attempting to install this product, if you're using Windows 8.1:

1. Make sure that you've installed the necessary character sets on your computer for either the Chinese Simple or Traditional languages (or both).
2. Disable ALL anti-viral and anti-malware services (e.g., Windows Defender, Spybot, McAfee, Norton and so on)
3. Make sure that you have an open internet connection rated at >= 800 kbps (you should have a firewall to protect you, as you're turning off your anti-virus)
4. Download the executables directly from Rosetta's AKAMAI portal. Visit the Rosetta site to find the most recent URLs for this. This is necessary because Amazon's executables may lead to you improperly installing the TotalE version of Rosetta, which will conflict with your ability to properly install the Language Training
5. Place all the executables and packages into a single directory and then COPY the "rsd" files into another completely separate path, in order to preserve these. 6. Change the properties of the Setup.exe to set its compatibility level to Win. 8.0 from Win. 8.1. The setup.exe was probably rushed out and may not be fully compatible with Win 8.1
7. Make sure that you review the Control Panel > Programs dialog, to ensure that there are no prior versions of Rosetta currently installed (this, of course, relates to attempting your first ever install)
8. Make sure that you have at least 3 GB of open space on your C drive. Rosetta uses the default drive and doesn't give you the opportunity to configure this to install the program elsewhere.

Man, have you guys used this yet? Drop the poorly-written slow-as-molasses LR and put aside C1Pro for awhile and give this a try! It's available for Windows, Mac, and Linux so you're afforded a bit of platform freedom with it. There's a trial version available on the home site as well.

The Corel site starts off the introductory blurb with \\"Corel® AfterShot(tm) Pro is a fast...\\" and as these kinds of blurbs typically go they're drastically understating the case. Running AfterShot Pro on my ancient 2006 MacPro1,1 (w/32GB RAM, and 8-cores of x5355 Xeon at 2.67GHz & GTX570) acts much faster than LR on my liquid-cooled 16-core 4+ GHz Boxx 8980 XTREME with dual Tesla cards and 32GB RAM!

All the usual raw processing tools plus some unexpected goodies are presented in a pretty slick highly customizable, gooey (GUI):

http://note.io/17LKc86

It's of course all non-destructive. The last 4 or 5 revision releases have offered OpenCL support as you can see from the image above. Totally sweet! It has layer masks for selective editing and processing. Layer brushing can be as accurate as 2 pixels and selection areas are sub-pixel accurate. It has options for independent layers which allow opacity and unique selection spline sets and/or brush strokes per layer. The selection splines can be edited at any time during editing or after saving the files out. I guess the spline data is saved in either of it's two kinds of XMP sidecar files. It sports a plug-in architecture but I haven't looked yet to see what APIs it's using nor if the plugs are compatible with those from/for other apps. Mine came with a souped up version of NoiseNinja and B&W processor with selective color capabilities.

http://note.io/1axsBVt

It supports catalogs which I personally dislike, and also OS hierarchal folder structures of your own devise - which is what I prefer. It uses just two user definable folders for all of its cache, work, proofs, previews, and profiles so it won't make a mess of things either. The review-and-select tools are similar to all other good PP apps I've tried so finding, sorting, and tagging stuff is done in the usual ways. Basically if you already know LR, CP1, or Aperture, there's no learning curve to deal with - just a HUGE speed increase and who doesn't want that? It has some nice output features but nothing others don't have IIRC. PDF files, Proof (Contact) Sheets, and so on. It also has a slide-show feature but it's fairly simplistic with just interval, border offsets, and so on as available options. No fancy wipes or anything but this is a RAW processor so I'm not sure how fitting something like wipes or etceteras, would be. It's got Versioning, Stacking, Keywording, Tagging, and Star Rating to help with progressive edit revisions and so forth. And the various tool pallets can be docked and floated for us multi-monitor users.

My little old MP1,1 with GTX570 can select, apply many many adjustments, and display GH2 RAW files in 0.27s or 3 FPS depending how you look at it. Processing, converting, and saving one raw-to-jpeg image at a time occurs in about 0.8 seconds with every slider and adjustment set to something other than the as-shot defaults. Batch processing 100 such 16mpx GH2 raw files took considerably less time with an average 0.63 seconds for each. That's fast in the extreme - given my machine spec!

So give this a try. DL the trial version, walk through all the preferences to optimize it for your particular system, then try out all the features, and see what you think. I have a feeling a lot of folks will be switching to this app. Me, I'm uninstalling LR all together - that's for sure! They've put together quite a system with hordes of free plug-ins and a fairly energetic forum community.

This review concerns the \\"downloading\\" of Excel 2013, letting Microsoft install it on your computer, and what may happen after that.  Maybe it's possible to download Excel 2013 from Amazon, but the comments I've read so far don't give me much confidence.  My experience regarding this downloading business (because Microsoft sure won't warn you): I tried purchasing and downloading Excel 2013 from the Microsoft Store and wasted my whole morning trying to do so.  I wanted to actually download the application as Microsoft advertised (they do say \\"download\\"), and downloading is what one typically does when one buys software online.  However, after talking to many confused people at Microsoft, it finally became clear that one cannot truly \\"download\\" because Microsoft won't allow it. Thus, I assume the same applies to Amazon, so beware.  Instead, Microsoft sends you a small executable file that connects your computer to its server, and then its server installs the program on your computer for you.  Although you buy their software (they say you technically just get their permission to use it), Microsoft prohibits you from downloading their executable application, -so don't plan on having it available for emergencies when your computer crashes.  The explanation is that they don't trust you, they fear that you might use Excel on a different computer without a license, and they'd prefer that you suffer the consequences of their anti-fraud policies as long as it means more money for them.  Who can blame them for fighting fraud.  But at my expense?  I don't think so!  I count on product reliability, and it can't be reliable if I don't have it, -if I can't reinstall it when I need it.  Remember, if you bought their software and you need to do a reinstall for whatever reason, you're responsible for figuring out how to connect to one of Microsoft's servers, how to get it to install the program on your computer again (which also means that you'd better have an Internet connection when you need it, and hope all goes well).  You may need to worry that they're giving you a different version (updates) that may or may not be compatible with your system (i.e. conflicts).  It also means that you've got to rely on Microsoft's servers being available when you need them, and hope that Microsoft is still servicing the version of Excel you want to reinstall, i.e. in other words, will it be possible to even get the software again from their servers if you need it in 3 years, 5 years or 10 years from now, and at what cost/inconvenience?  I'm sure they're figuring that the majority of people will be inconvenienced enough that they'd rather just pay more money for a new, slightly ugraded version (nice marketing), -and tough luck if you happen to want to keep your \\"old\\" version or need the older version again for some compatibility reason.  Imagine if all software vendors took this approach, and you bought another computer, or had to reinstall your software for some reason, and you had to figure out how to connect to each of a dozen other servers again (one for each vendor), and each one required a different password, username, key number, mother's maiden name, pet's name or whatever else...so you might eventually get your software installed again, -if lucky.  I'm not \\"modern\\" enough for that.  But, if this is someone's idea of \\"survice,\\" -let them go for it!  I cancelled my order for Excel 2013.  Figured that there are plenty of other good spreadsheets available without the expense and hassle.

Sorry if I'm too late on this - what's happening to you sounds like a problem I had a few years ago concerning BofA. I went through all the same hassle (sending logs, Intuit blaming the bank, etc.) until someone who knew told me about this way to reset a key register of financial institutions:

First, turn off online access for the troubled account. Then:
1. Open Tools > Online center
2. When open, hover cursor on over \\"contact info\\" at the top
3. While there, hold down CTRL+F3 as you click on \\"contact info\\"
4. A hidden list of financial institutions comes up
5. Find the bank that problem concerns (this is a more fundamental delete than just disabling online account access)
6. Select to \\"Delete\\" that bank's record from this list (don't worry, it will get it again when you set up online access again)
7. Then close, restart Quicken, and go back and re-initialize online access for the troubled account

This is basically a fundamental reset of your Quicken's record concerning that bank, it can kick out a hidden banking profile that's been corrupted or is now misdirected (as was my own problem).

This is of course a preliminary review (written Dec 9 based on use in the last few days). At this time one can't do more than a rough cut estimate of the tax return -- the IRS forms aren't finalized, the state forms aren't available, and of course the various income reports (W2, 1099, etc.) aren't out yet.

I don't have a super complicated tax situation this year: it just requires some things that a good tax program should handle easily. So far this program seems to do just fine. I found it easy to use, and found that imports from Quicken and from TXF files worked without any problems. Schedules A, B, and D worked just fine, and the related screens were easy to use and understand. Excess FICA was calculated correctly, as was the child tax credit. The AMT calculation does of course remain weirdly complicated (once a year I mutter to myself about all politicians in DC), but the program does take care of it with no apparent problems.

I used TaxCut last year -- chose it over TurboTax just because of cost, and was quite satisfied. I'm not convinced this year either that you get value for the extra you pay for TT. (Incidentally, note that if you have investment income you probably need to get TT Premium, so the price would be nearly double that of HRB Deluxe.)

A warning I wrote in my review last year seems worth repeating: Don't expect a tax program to apply tax laws correctly in all circumstances; for anything at all out of the ordinary, make sure you double-check against an IRS guide or another guide like JK Lasser's. The folks who design and write and test the programs make mistakes, too. And for the same reason, give the calculations a sanity check, don't just use the program blindly, or you could get tripped up by a software bug that wasn't caught.

I will update this review in Jan/Feb when I've had a chance to do more with it.

Interestingly, TTD is also noticeably slower starting up than HRBD. Don't know why.

The one advantage TT does have over HRB is on coverage of automated downloads: TT can download your 1099 info from a larger set of institutions than can HRB. W2 downloads look the same between the two. This does save some time, and could be sufficient to be a decider for some. Norton set me up with a new subscription with 366 days remaining until I would need to renew and cheated me out of 12 days.

Other issues with Norton: The Norton tool bar has an icon for sharing information on Facebook that cannot be removed. The Facebook requirement reduces the available menu options on \\"Vault Open\\" menu by 2. Apparently Norton reserves two spaces on the \\"Vault Open\\" menu for Facebook. I deleted any Facebook reference from my list but the \\"Vault Open\\" menu now assigns what appear to be random log on entries where the Facebook options were.

Update: I logged on to my Norton Account and clicked the \\"Renew\\" button next to my existing subscription and found that I could extend my existing subscription by one year with no loss in days remaining for $19. This is a dollar less that I paid for the product code from Amazon. This appears to be the better deal since there is no loss of remaining days. If you have a Norton account, check this out before buying a product code only.

If you are a current Quicken user faced with a forced upgrade, version 2013 is now R10 and is no better than 2010. My prior upgrades were 2004, 2007, and 2010.

I am a user since 1988. My working files involve 60,000 records. Overall, I checked over 100,000 records spanning split files going back to 1990.

I've seen a lot change with Quicken, many are painful. Periodic upgrades do make sense given its Internet centric operation because HTML, encryption, security protocols, and more, change and improve and Quicken must adopt these changes. Alas, to users most of these are invisible and behind the scenes. If they are, Intuit should detail them, because they are more important than all the advertised reporting modes in all versions of Quicken; I can and did do most of these myself, but many were eventually ruined by upgrades; so now I use only Quicken's reports and cross check its subtotals.

Since 2010, Quicken uses the slower Microsoft's .NET framework for coding, which consumes more memory and disk space to add capability and stability. Screen drawing is also slower, but all of these are a .NET issue. Computers should find these added needs inconsequential if these machines run games and 720p movies easily. I've not had problems with data syncing, slow response, bugs, lost data, corrupt files etc., despite my 6+ year old quad core computer.

I've never upgraded to a first release of a new version to avoid bugs, nor overwritten a prior version. Always make a full system backup, a system restore point, validate your file, make a Quicken file backup, then do a fresh install in a new directory, then start Quicken as a virgin program then import a copy of your prior data. To be safe I remove the data files from the PC while Quicken installs. This leads to the least, if not problem free upgrade and an effortless path back to the old version or old files should an upgrade bomb. Although I received 2013 Release 1.0, online files were available to upgrade my 2013 to Release 10, and I've had no problems with Quicken in 12 years.

To avoid hassles with problematic license installs, I obtained the CD version not the download version as it comes without added cost, to insure I can install as many copies as I need should I have a PC disaster. So far, I've installed it in 2 PCs easily and problem free.

The GUI is essentially unchanged, but its noticeable cleaner, but its still far more like 2010, and clearly not worth paying for. Many of the shortcomings of 2010 are still there, that I no longer use but remain compatible with prior versions, e.g. you can send electronic payments 3 ways, a 1990s \\"online banking\\" interface, the checking register, or a separate checkbook app.

One noticeable improvement is that downloads are now concurrent, rather than one at a time; so it goes faster and no longer locks up and needs a restart, as it did for even the latest 2010 version.

The new budget app has its quirks, as have prior versions in the past, so as Quicken veteran expecting always the worst, I tweaked it to work properly.

Over the decades, some accounts have ceased to function properly, what I did was mothball old accounts, use the account Quicken prefers and zero the mothballed balance. This year, I've had problems with paypal imports. This causes no short term problems for accounting, but it creates issues when analyzing patterns spanning many years. As a last straw, you can import QIF or QFX files to accounts formatted as \\"other\\" asset or liability.

The new user should avoid Quicken and try many of its competitors as they have made substantial gains since 2010, e.g. GnuCash or Moneydance. I am running GnuCash simultaneously and migrating slowly. The only concern with competitors is direct downloads and payments, because logon credentials should have the best possible security given risk of online account theft; to date there are no reports of Quicken users being hacked and compromised, whether from their home desktops or Quicken's servers; that to me, is a potential major plus Intuit fails to capitalize on.o reports of Quicken users being hacked and compromised, whether from their home desktops or Quicken's servers; that to me, is a potential major plus Intuit fails to capitalize on.

Ok... So I read all of the negative reviews and decided to try anyway. Let me explain that I wanted a way to download my checking transactions from my bank, categorize them, and save them for review at tax time. I'm not sure that I would use Quicken to work with my stocks. I generally work with my broker's website to do that. I used Quicken extensively many years ago on a PC, but gave it up when I went to a Mac (and I ain't going back).

Having set expectations fairly low, I gave it a go. Firstly, it doesn't resemble the old Windows Quicken from years ago. I worked with Quicken on PC a few years back and it appeared to have far too many bells and whistles for me. I never did derive anything positive from following my stocks with Quicken.

My credit union doesn't allow Quicken to log in directly, so I have to manually download transactions and upload them into Quicken. This was straight forward so I picked up a couple of months of data without much difficulty and imported into Quicken without any problem. Within 10 minutes, I had changed a few categories to suit my particular needs, categorized each entry, and reconciled 2 months worth of data. Next, I imported 2 credit cards and categorized and reconciled them.

One of the reviews I read said that the user was unable to transfer from one account to another. Using the 'Columns' button at the bottom, I added a 'Transfer' column. On the entries that were actually transfers (paid my Visa and AmEx from my checking account), I clicked on the Transfer column within the entry and selected the account that the money was transferred to and Quicken said it found the corresponding entry and reconciled the entry for me. Very simple.

One neat feature is that I can add documents to a transaction. My bank no longer sends checks back to me, but instead allows you to look at a copy of the check on-line. I have made a habit of downloading these onto my PC and now, directly on the transaction line, I can create a link to the picture of the check. Pretty simple.

Thus far, I haven't read or looked at any documentation and seem to be able to do what I want.... But I haven't tried to bring in my stock portfolio, either. Also, I don't 'write checks' from within Quicken, either. If you are looking at a fairly simple program to track and categorize your checking and credit card transactions, then Quicken 2015 for Mac might just be for you.

Another issue is the use of the Cloud. I am not a fan of sending financial data across the Cloud. I would prefer the ability to sync using a direct connect or transfer between my mobile app and my computer.

Due to transactions processing at my bank, the true available balance is not displayed in the mobile app. For example, I may have a transaction for a purchase appear on my bank's website as \\"Processing\\" rather than \\"Posted.\\" Quicken mobile will track the account balance of all Posted transactions, but doesn't include the \\"Processing\\" transactions. I realize that Processing transactions may change, but I don't get a true sense of what is actually available to me to spend. I don't know if that is a problem that Quicken can solve or not since it seems to have more to do with how the bank operates.

Overall, this is a step in the right direction. It isn't perfect and I waffled between giving the product 3 or 4 stars. I went with 3 because it appears to be heading in the right direction, but needs some work.

I had roughly 52 GB that plummeted to zero. I ended up closing Photoshop without saving changes, and the OS restored 1 GB of space every few seconds. Maybe this new release behaves differently with Solid State Drive technology, but am unable to prove it. May be an unusual configuration thing with my late 2007 Mac Pro, which probably was not natively capable of Solid State Drive support. It only works because of the standard pin connectors. It is not even properly seated in my tower, but is secure enough the drive won't slip out onto the logic board. Enough said. Photoshop works very well, as said, but this latest release on Mac has dropped the 32-bit plug-ins, meaning Variations (for example) no longer works because it is not supported in x64 mode. This behavior does not happen on my PC, but that is a conventional platter drive that obviously runs very slowly in comparison. Recommended? Yes. Very few complaints. It mightbe an unusual auto-configuration thing my Mac decided to allocate drive space as if it were RAM, and my theory is because the drive's read/write speed is comparable to the DDR2 667 MHz modules in it. It saves files about the same speed, but renders data very quickly. Do not know about the 3D features (my Mac Pro is too old to support it), but on the PC, the 3D features are a bit sluggish like the CC version. That said, it might be the drive access thing. Any ideas? Thanks for reading.

I downloaded this dictionary just after I bought a new MacBook Pro laptop two weeks ago (October 2011).  So far, I've been rather disappointed.  First, the main use I had in mind for the dictionary was to aid me in reading Spanish-language web sites, esp. newspapers.  I wanted to be able to click on a word in the text to have the definition pop up in English.  The dictionary advertises this capability. However, I've had a devil of a time setting up this capability.  First, to use a mouse short-cut, the only \\"click\\" available to set up is the three-finger click or the four-finger click (whatever that is!).  Unfortunately, my brand new top-of-the-line Apple wireless \\"Magic Mouse\\" does not support a 3-finger click!  So a program advertised as being \\"the Mac version\\" does not support current Mac hardware...  I had to search the web, and was able to download a mini-program to add the three-finger click option to the Magic Mouse and touch-pad, but this has been a poor fix: every time i accidentally brush 3 fingers against the mouse, an annoying Ultralingua pop-up appears on the screen.  The alternative to the mouse-click to set up the pop-up definition capability is a keyboard shortcut - but setting up the preferences for this has been difficult.  I was not able to set it up, so I took my Mac to the Apple store during one of my 1-to-one tutoring sessions, and the program still would not let us type a shortcut into the proper field in the preferences window. (Later, at home, the program allowed me to type in a shortcut command to use this - so the program does not appear to be very dependable or stable).  Next, as to the quality of the definitions provided.  So far, this has been disappointing as well.  First, the definitions provided tend to be of the one-word variety - if, like me, you're a more advanced student of Spanish, you know that one-word translations tend to be frustrating and inadequate.  Second, a good percentage of the words I've looked up do not appear in the dictionary.  Again, since i'm a more advanced student, I'm trying to look up more uncommon words, so the dictionary would appear to be of greater use to more beginning students.  Examples - I looked up the word \\"socaire,\\" which I've run across a number of times in general-interest newspaper articles - does not appear in the dictionary.  I tried to look up the word \\"revuelta\\", in the sense of a revolt or uprising.  This fairly common word does not appear in the dictionary - instead, the word \\"revuelto\\" (masculine form) was suggested, with the one-word definition \\"stir-fry.\\" Not even close, no cigar!  In short, I've been fairly disappointed with the product.  With my old PC, I had a pretty convenient short-cut set up for pop-up translation: with Firefox browser, I was able to use a right-click on the mouse to come up with a good definition from the excellent Word Reference web site.  However, this capability does not seem to exist for Apple's Safari browser, nor for the Firefox version for Macs that I downloaded. Another experience that's left me with fond memories for my old PC!

I only use MS Visio for working with database models so my review is limited to that one type of diagram.

I just don't know what Microsoft is thinking. Clearly, they do not listen to the customers that do serious database work with Visio. They removed the ability to reverse-engineer. In Visio 2010, I could connect to a database, reverse-engineer that into a database model, and then make changes to update the design. Not any more.

No more support for specifying data types.

Foreign keys are no longer placed automatically when designing 1:M relationships.

Primary keys are no longer underlined, which means you must leave the clunky \\"PK\\" symbol next to the attribute if you want to indicate primary keys. Even worse, now the PK and FK symbols are in boxes so they take up even more space on the diagram. Take it another step -- they have separate columns for \\"PK\\" and \\"FK\\" now so the left side of an entity is even wider to support the two columns for the symbol boxes.

The end result is that fitting more than six or so entities on a page is difficult. How many real, business databases have only six or so entities? None.

Specifying attributes for an entity was previously done in a tabular window so you could just to keep entering attributes. Now, it requires adding attributes like you were adding text boxes to the entity.

It looks like the database diagrams in Visio were redesigned by graphic artists who know a lot about making the screen look pretty on a tablet, but nothing about how the software is actually used. After a couple of months trying to work with it, I've uninstalled Visio 2013 and have gone back to my previous version.

As a new user, I found Quicken 2013 difficult to get fully up and running. Specifically, it was difficult to add enough past transaction history into Quicken to perform reasonable analyses (two years in my case). The connection to my bank and download of accounts was a snap, but since Wells Fargo only provided the last 90 days of transactions and VISA only the last 60 days, I spent the next week trying to learn how to import the rest. After several failed attempts, exhaustive internet searches for help, and after purchasing several converters from ProperSoft, I finally got everything to work.

Recommendations to new users: don't use the automatic setup feature. Instead: (1) choose the date range you want* and download QFX files from your bank to your computer, (2) import the files into Quicken using Web Connect (not Express Web Connect) - this prevents connection to your bank during import, (3) make sure the imports look good, (4) go to Tools/Account-List, and for each account click Edit, go to the Online Services tab, and change the connection method to Express Web Connect or Direct Connect as desired. At this point you are ready for your first automatic update with your bank. Do the update and check the accounts (you will probably need to change your \\"Opening Balance\\" to get the right current balance).

* Note that to be able to import QFX files using Web Connect, my bank (and Quicken) required that the desired start date and balance correspond to the start date and balance on a past monthly statement.

Adding sufficient Credit Account history is similar but a little harder. Your bank may not even let you download more than 60 days directly, so you will first need to manually cut and paste data from old statements into a spreadsheet, format the data for CSV to QIF conversion, buy a converter (ProperSoft CSV2QIF converter works well), convert the data, and import the QIF file into Quicken.

Recommendations to Quicken (and associated financial institutions): (1) provide at least two years of transaction history for Quicken automatic set up (this includes VISA and the like), (2) if you can't do recommendation 1, then add more comprehensive set up instructions and add capability for Quicken to import csv files (or provide converters with new orders).

Check the listing here to really understand editions, as some users are accidentally purchasing the wrong one. What you are buying here is either a 'Download' stored in your Amazon digital locker complete with license key or a 'Key Card'--plastic card with the license key printed on it that is shipped to you. Both download and key-card involve downloading Office.

Also, Office 2013 is NOT compatible with Windows XP or Vista. It requires you to have Windows 7 or 8.

The Short Form
There were some good ideas behind the improvements to Office 2013, but poor execution, a confusing bid to sell Office 365, and licensing issues (that have since been improved) have tripped up this version of Office. You'll survive with it on a new computer, but there aren't a lot of reasons to upgrade if you already have an existing version of Office.

The Good
If you're a long-time user of Office, there aren't a lot of incentives in Office 2013 to make you want to jump onto the bandwagon apart from the fact that it really does load faster and respond fairly snappily, even on older hardware. The UI is another step beyond what Office 2010 did, offering a flatter-looking ribbon, more stuff dumped into the ribbon, and yet more of those full-screen interface menus that now resemble the 'Modern UI' front-end of Windows 8 and Windows Phone. There are little pleasantries, like files flowing more seamlessly in and out of SkyDrive, and the way the cursor tracks as you type is a surprisingly nice detail. One of the things Microsoft has been trying to do is make your Windows Live/Microsoft/Hotmail/X-Box/SkyDrive account a one-stop shop for all things Microsoft, and so if you set up Windows and/or Office to tie directly into that, little fringe benefits like the aforementioned SkyDrive are dropped into your programs.

Installation of Office 2013 is a breeze--it is surprisingly fast, in minutes if you've already downloaded the files. It's also slightly simpler than earlier versions, getting quickly to the \\"Install now/Customize\\" screen. The first step is a doozy, though: you might start off with an Office 365 prompt that tells you to enter in the e-mail address associated with your Office install. Pay attention to the \\"I want to use a Product Key\\" link on that screen: it flips you from, \\"I'm about to accidentally kick off a 90-day Office 365 Trial\\" to \\"I have a license key, now where do I type it in?\\". The first time I did this I thought this was about tying Office to my Microsoft account, so I went that route and ended up getting e-mails about my Office 365 Trial, how I can use Office via a browser, etc., etc.; and after the trial, I realized my mistake because Office 'deactivated'. I had to go back in and properly 'Activate' office with my key.

The Bad, Lumped In With The Ugly
Unfortunately, we then come to the 'look and feel' and that's where things start to literally get ugly. Office 2013 has a default color palette of \\"One color, black text, and white all over the place.\\" There are two other color schemes, but no other way to customize the interface nor any downloadable themes. All three options, \\"White\\", \\"Light Gray\\", and \\"Dark Gray\\" end up adding to the eyestrain. The menus we lost in the Ribbon of 2007 to 2007's circular candy-button were put back in Office 2010 as colored tabs, and in 2013 they SHOUT AT YOU IN ALL CAPS. \\"FILE HOME VIEW...\\" they say, and I feel like my dad just sent me an e-mail.

Because of the work I do, I often have to have two versions of Office installed at the same time. Just like 2007 and 2010, it's possible to have a dual install, but some products are going to screw up. My Outlook 2010 was completely removed, and MS Project (sold separately) still really hates to sit on the same machine with another version. I now have regular licensing dust-ups, where one product or another claims that there was a problem in activating Office and starts running some sort of setup screen. I then have to close everything, reboot, and run through activating Office again. My fault for being weird and running two versions, but I tell you this so you know to avoid trying to keep both on the same machine--pick one or the other.

The Bottom Line

I've been using Quicken since the 90s, and up until today had been using Quicken 2011. Along with my email client, Quicken is the most important software program on my PC. So when I was notified today that Quicken 2013 was available, I went online to see what new features were available. When I saw the availability to view my Quicken data on my iPad, I immediately purchased Quicken 2013 from Amazon (download), solely for that iPad capability.

To my shock, only after purchasing & installing Quicken 2013 did I learn that the Mobile App capability does NOT work with non-US accounts.

I accept that quite likely most Quicken users live in the US, with all their accounts being US Dollar accounts, and therefore this problem does not apply.

In my case, I track 10 bank accounts & credit cards. Of these, only 3 are US dollar accounts or credit cards, and these are only secondary accounts & card, rarely used, and not what I would view often on my iPad. So the sole reason for me upgrading to Quicken 2013 for the Mobile App capability was useless and therefore a waste of my money.

I must mention, though, that during the setup of my Quicken Cloud account, I was told that \\"at this time\\" Quicken Mobile App support only works with US bank account & credit cards. So hopefully Intuit are working on this limitation, and soon I'll be able to view non-US bank accounts & cards on my iPad. :-)

I just wanted to post this review, so that anyone else with non-US accounts & cards are aware of this limitation.

Having said that, the following are my impressions of the iPad App itself .....

Overall, it's not great, but for a 1st release it's OK.

When I open up Quicken on my PC, I have it set to show me all my (non-hidden) bank accounts & credit cards, along with my current balance for each. There is no way (that I've found) to have my Quicken iPad App do the same on the opening screen. It is possible, though, and takes just 1 finger press to call up that information, so I'm not complaining. It's just that the initial display screen shows items that I never use, such as Spending by Category, Budgets, etc.

A bigger issue with the Quicken iPad display is that when bank accounts & credit cards are selected, the display states that it's showing the \\"Current Balance\\" in the top-right corner, but the amount displayed is actually the \\"Ending Balance\\". To explain, I have Quicken on my PC set to automatically enter in bills into my register 65 days ahead of time, so I can see at a glance any upcoming credits/payments/debits, etc. In my desktop register, each entry shows the Current Balance on each line. At the bottom of the register, both Current Balance and Ending Balance are shown. In my case, the Ending Balance is irrelevant - only the Current Balance is of interest to me. And I have my accounts list on the left side display Current Balance (the other option is Ending Balance, for those who prefer that). But there's no option yet in the iPad App to select Current Balance to be displayed.

Again, this is only the 1st release of the Quicken iPad App, so I'm optimistic that hopefully in the near future it will become more customizable.

And hopefully soon the Quicken iPad App will support non-US bank accounts and cards. Until then it's useless for me, and not worth my upgrade earlier today to Quicken 2013.

This program includes 1,500 Thai words, written in both Thai and transliterated English. The program includes audio, so you can hear how each word is pronounced. The words are divided into categories like "airport," "changing money," "clothes," etc. You can study the words either within those categories, or by adding them to your "wordbank" and then studying your wordbank.
If you want to study the words in your wordbank in the form of flashcards, each word in the wordbank will be presented to you in written Thai. When you click on flashcard, the English translation is given, and you have the option of hearing the Thai pronunciation.

There are two aspects of this program that I didn't like. First, the vocabulary selection is terrible. Too much of it is tourist specific. Even if you were using the course to prepare for a trip to Bangkok, you don't need to know the Thai words for "duty free," "hangar" and "boarding gate" to travel around the country. And that type of vocabulary is worthless for a beginning or intermediate student. What percentage of your daily conversations involve airplane hangars or duty free shops? In short, there aren't enough useful verbs in this program. Second, the flashcards always appear in the same order. So, for example, if you're studying colors, you will know after you've been through the cards a couple times that green comes after blue, even if you don't actually recognize the Thai word for green.

But, having aired my complaints, I wish I had had a program like this 20 years ago when I was studying Russian, or 25 years ago when I was studying French. Studying Thai vocabulary without audio is almost pointless. So this program provides an inexpensive way to practice reading and pronouncing Thai while building your vocabulary.

Download and installation was a breeze and once I ran the software it checked for any updates and quickly applied those. Since I was new to TurboTax I had to enter all of my information but I didn't find this too hard - just needed to know the birthdays and SSN's of all my family members. The cool thing about this process is that it takes you step by step through each different area - and I found it as easy as it was updating my information for my CPA.

I was really worried about having to enter all my business data - because with having a business with large revenues and a lot of different categorized expenses I thought it would be overwhelming. But since I had a Schedule C it was very easy to enter revenues and then expenses in each category - and I found that it made more sense with me doing it than it did to me before when my CPA did it. And again Turbo Tax walked me through each step of the process and made sure I didn't miss anything.

After completing my tax return with TurboTax - which did take me about an hour or two - just because I was meticulous - I then compared it to my previous year's tax return to make sure everything looked right and that I didn't miss anything. I spent another hour or so comparing data and calculations and found that TurboTax did everything like how my CPA did it - and it now made sense to me why things were done the way they were done. The crazy thing is that I have to spend at least an hour or two each year getting all my information together for my CPA for him to do my tax return - yet instead this year I just spent that time putting that information in TurboTax. Pros:

1. Cheap - $69 to help organize and file your taxes for a business is a steal - especially compared to the $435 I was paying for a CPA.

3. Convenient - You can do this when you want to do it and save at any point and pick up where you left off.

Cons:

2. You don't get the protection and help of a CPA.
3. If your business is a partnership, LLC, or corporation you will need to use the more separate and more expensive TurboTax Business software (I'm currently a sole proprietorship).

Conclusion:

Yes, you don't get the protection and help of a CPA, but for me doing it yourself and knowing and understanding the data just makes it that much more rewarding. You don't have to worry about making sure you get all the tax breaks and credits you qualify for because TurboTax handles that for you - assuming you enter all of your data correctly. First, and most important, I HIGHLY recommend downloading the 30-day free trial version direct from IGGsoftware dot com. If you buy it from Amazon or the App Store, there is NO 90-day guarantee available, per the iBank website and other reviewers here!!  Sorry Amazon, but it's important that people get a feel for this program to determine if it's going to work for them. If not, they could be in for an unpleasant surprise. Apparently, neither Apple nor Amazon provide refunds for downloaded products, and IGG can't or doesn't want to provide refunds for product downloaded from anybody else. Interestingly, a Quicken for Mac 2015 purchase downloaded from Amazon IS refundable, although the process requires sending Intuit an e-mail with your Amazon order confirmation, and they will send you a paper check in 3-4 weeks. So, if you want to buy through Amazon, and refundability is important, I suggest purchasing Quicken.  Next, it's important to understand the distinction iBank makes between "Direct Connect" and "Direct Access". "Direct Connect" is included in the purchase price and works with many banks and brokerages. "Direct Access" is an additional monthly, quarterly, or annual subscription. I think you have to try it out to see if your bank works with Direct Connect. Another reason to go with the free trial from IGG. Some of my banks are not supported by Direct Connect, but I can download QFX files and import them. For one of my banks, it supports neither. For this situation, iBank includes a built-in web browser that takes you to the bank website. Once on your bank's site, you can download your transactions and they will automatically import. This uses QIF format, and the import works fine. There was a bug importing QIF files, but this bug was fixed in a March 2015 upgrade to version 5.5.2. Another one of my banks is supported by Direct Access, but I haven't paid for the subscription. iBank doesn't give me the option to set up a website link to this bank. I must go to Safari or Chrome, log in, download the file, and import it manually. Fortunately, it's not an account I must update every day. One note about Direct Access: Quicken for Windows disables all online services 3 years from date of purchase. Since you must buy Quicken every 3 years, there's essentially a subscription built into the price. All software upgrades for iBank will be free until version 6.0 is released, and they have provided discounts in the past to upgrade to a new major version. Quicken for Mac 2015 doesn't have a scheduled date of discontinuation, but I guess that's up to the whims of Intuit.  I haven't fully explored iBank, but I've noticed some quirks. For example, I happened to set up my mortgage loan information on the same day that a payment is due. Now, iBank doesn't want to let me post the payment. Maybe it will tomorrow??? I would assume it will work for subsequent months. At least, unlike Quicken for Mac 2015, it can do loan amortization and create the split transactions. [EDIT: I contacted customer support. I had to turn reminders on by selecting the loan account, then "Show Loan Settings..." from the "Account" menu. Then, the loan transactions were available for posting. So, my mortgage payments are showing up now.] One tool that's missing: an paycheck wizard to set up the splits using common predefined fields. However, I believe iBank does save a template when you set up a split, so if you are tracking two paychecks, it is probably easy to use the template from one to set up the other.  I have a savings plan that uses privately managed investment funds without ticker symbols. Quicken for Windows (and Mac) is able to figure out the updated share price from, I assume, the number of shares held and the value of the position. iBank can connect to the bank and download transactions, but it doesn't do the math to figure out the current share price. I assume the information is in the file that both iBank and Quicken download, so iBank must be lacking the proper code. I can manually update the prices by looking at the plan website and entering a quote, but that is less convenient.  Other reviewers have mentioned that the reports are not clickable. This is true. I sure would like to see what those "uncategorized expenses" are in that expense report by clicking on the line. The reports seem designed for reading or printing only; they are not interactive.  There are some "how-to" videos on the IGG website. If you download the product from IGG, it comes with a full PDF manual for the program, which I think is available as web pages on the website as well. I don't know if the Amazon download includes the manual. I have not contacted IGG customer support, so I can't comment on how good or bad it is. Most of my questions have been answered by reading the manual or searching the web. EDIT: Per my comment above, I did contact IGG support using their live chat. The support rep pointed me in the right direction. Wait time for support was about 10-15 minutes, and it took about 2 minutes to figure out the problem. I believe all of their support is by live chat and email, not phone.  I didn't use the software enough during the free trial to be sure I want it, but I used it enough to know that I might buy it if there were no other options (thus the 3 stars). I've bought Quicken for Mac 2015, and I'm not enthusiastic about it, either. I might exercise my 60-day refund option. In the end, I may go back to Boot Camp with Windows 7, and buy Quicken for Windows 2015, I might use Quicken for Mac 2015, or I might purchase iBank. I'm just not sure right now.

QuickBooks Pro allows for the management of multiple business entities and sources of business income.  Along with this diversity is the ability to create a chart of accounts that works for you, enabling you to report the info entered in various formats to suit your needs.

If you use TurboTax for your personal taxes and are expecting a similar experience (as I was), you'll be OK, but be aware that businesses taxes are more complex and the software reflects that. It doesn't walk you through as many decisions--you need to know how your business is set up and be ready to answer questions about your structure. I didn't find the tool tips and documentation as strong as the personal edition. I eventually figured things out, but it took a bit of Googling.

All in, I can definitely recommend TurboTax Business for small, simple businesses. If you've got anything of real size, get an accountant. The TurboTax website even says they're not ideal if your revenue is >$250K.

I purchased this software on December 13 based on the guarantee published on their web site:

\\"Risk-Free 200% Guarantee Means You Can't Lose. If you are not completely satisfied with the quality of your Cook'n Software, I will refund your purchase! In fact, I will go one step further and buy you the recipe software product of your choice.\\"

I evaluated the software for two weeks and on December 26, I send an email to the address provided in my order confirmation stating that I would like a refund. All the relevant order information was included. I know they received the email because I received an out-of-the-office message stating they would reply after the holidays. In that email, I provided three reasons for my decision which I've listed below and indicated that I would like them to purchase the software of my choice 'Living Cookbook'.

As of March 4, I had not received either a refund or the software product of my choice despite three additional emails to the company. One on January 22, one on February 10 and finally one on February 11.

On March 4, I filed a dispute with American Express and less than 24 hours later I received a refund, however, I was not provided with the \\"software product of my choice\\". So much for the 200% guarantee.

I am using 'Living Cookbook' and find it a far superior product at less than half the cost of Cook'N.

Here are the reasons I chose to return the product for a refund:

1) When I view a recipe in 'Living Cookbook', I am able to see both the recipe ingredients, directions and nutrition information all at the same time on the same page. With Cook'N I have to click to a different page and scroll over to see the report of the nutrition data. The report includes all nutrition not just the summary normally included. There is no way to view it all on the same page.

2) When I print a recipe with 'Living Cookbook', the format is clean and simple and the nutrition information is automatically included. With Cook'N I have to navigate to a special print configuration page and manually setup the configuration to include nutrition data each and every time I want to print a recipe. Clearly a lot more work.

3) I purchased the 'Living Cookbook' import add-on for Cook'N and it failed to correctly import my recipe database. Specifically, it failed to import the folder hierarchy and lumped all the recipes together in general categories, nearly useless.

'Living Cookbook' is a far better engineered product and they have taken into consideration user friendliness and efficiency. Cook'N appears to have a lot more bells and whistles, but that about all they are - bells and whistles NOT substance.

Four e-mails to the company failed to obtain a refund, but one call to American Express worked like a charm. Ask yourself whether you'll have to call American Express to get tech support if something goes wrong?.

This may not be as sophisticated a program as the \\"professional\\" versions, but for my purposes it's been great. The 2-d floor plan view works smoothly - and the \\"dollhouse\\" view is a good way to check if the flat floor plan really makes sense. Zooming and tilting only took a few minutes to master. My only problem so far is that the terrain function was hard to understand - thus the 4 instead of 5 stars.   This program most likely wouldn't satisfy the professional architect or contractor, but in terms of being able to produce a floor plan that I can tinker with, and print out to take to my contractor, I like it very well. It's fun to work with - as addictive as any game. A good value for the price.
