I was looking for a Windows 8 product to replace my Ulead Videostudio 11, which sadly does not support my 64 bit Windows 8.  Unfortunately, Corel bought Ulead and the follow-on products are FUBAR.  Anyway, I downloaded the trial version (6.1.11)to evaluate it.  My primary use is to create DVDs with slideshows that contain images set to music and video clips spliced together.  You can see some examples of those at [...]. I absolutely LOVE the interface on this product....the expandable timeline is the best feature.  Videostudio had a nice time line, but it wasn't expandable.  Nice transition effects, intuitive use of the timeline, captions, anything you could want.  I was impressed!!  The first problem I ran into was that music played on after I set it to end.  Turns out that is a \\"feature\\" that will fill the play time of the slides automatically; including playing over the audio on the video clips! Be sure to go to \\"Settings\\" and turn that off before you start using the product or it will have you scratching your head until you figure it out. With such a nice timeline, I can see no reason for this \\"feature\\", much less have the default \\"on\\", but once you know about it, no big deal. The next \\"feature\\" I encountered was that there is apparently a built-in audio fade on the video clips.  This means that if there is narrative on the very end of a clip, you will lose it in the audio fade. This also creates problems when you are splicing clips together with no transition. I could find no way to turn this off.  That alone made the product unusable for me, but I guess if you are using only images, you don't care. After creating a slideshow, it looked really nice....beautiful preview window, you can drag the time line pointer to play anywhere in the slideshow, delete transitions, text, really nice!  OK, time to try burning a DVD.  I first created a .iso file (DVD image) The product creates some really nice DVD menus, with the option to use images, thumbnails, add your own text, etc.  Again I was impressed! The .iso image played nicely on my PC with VLC.  Next I burned a DVD from the .iso file.  Again it played nicely on my PC with VLC. The final test was to see if it worked on my TOSHIBA BD3000 Blu-Ray DVD player.  Playing it there resulted in some serious issues.  First, the audio was choppy and broken up badly...VERY badly! The DVD had three slideshows on it because I wanted to see how the menus worked.  Here again, serious problems. The DVD menu button, which returns you to the root menu did not work.  The only functional keys were Pause, Play, Up and Down. Next, you could select any of the three slideshows, but it would always play the first one on the menu. Just to be sure I wasn't having problems my DVD drivers or burner, I repeated the above tests on a Windows 7 machine with the same results.  Totally unusable DVD burn.    After trading a number of emails with a very nice lady who promptly responded to my support request, she finally said \\"We don't support Blu-Ray players very well\\".  I was somewhat taken aback, since just about everyone who buys a player now buys Blu-Ray. Without Blu-Ray player support, I can't use it. It also does not burn Blu-Ray DVDs....but I could live with that, although that needs to be added.    There is no built in help text....the only help without a support ticket requires you to thrash through a lot of on-line user posts, faqs, etc. which are kinda mixed in with other products and previous products and previous versions, so it was difficult to find an answer to a question or problem.  Although the product is very intuitive and except for the audio issues, very easy to use, a PDF file or built-in help file would be nice.    IMHO, This product shows great promise, but needs a few more versions to solve the problems above before it's usable for me.  By the way, you can buy a license for $35 if you shop around.  The trial version is fully functional...it just puts a banner across the DVD when you burn it.I would be be willing to pay a LOT more than that if they ever solve the problems....GREAT user interface.

Well, taxes are done, and I’d like to share my first-time experience with H & R Deluxe with One State.  I had previously used Turbotax Deluxe with One State for over 20 yrs (since it was distributed on floppy disks).  Over the years, the price of Turbotax has shot up, and the software has become bloated.  And this year, Turbotax pulled a faux pas extraordinaire that caused many loyal users like myself to desert to alternatives.  I bought the PC download version of H & R Deluxe with One State from Amazon for $29.99.  A good price.  Installation went without a hitch (I’m running Windows 7 Home).  Importing the 2013 Turbotax returns also went without a hitch.  The user interface is similar to the Turbotax user interface before Turbotax introduced the GPS interface.  For me that’s good news, because I consider the GPS interface to be bloated.  I prepared a federal and a NY state return for my daughter.  NY requires electronic filing if you use major tax prep software.  And NY requires that there be no fee for electronic filing.  I electronically filed my daughter’s federal and NY state returns without a hitch.  The software includes 5 federal electronic filings without additional fees; state electronic filings normally cost $19.95 each, but the software properly recognized that there is no charge for a NY state electronic filing.  If I needed to file only a single state return, I would rate this product a 5.  As a side note, H & R has far fewer updates than Turbotax; not sure whether that’s good or bad.  I downgraded the rating to a 3, however, for the way the product handles (or, rather, mishandles) filings with two state returns.  First off, the software to prepare an additional state return costs a whopping $39.95 each; and that does not include electronic filing.  But this was the first year in which I had to file both a NJ (resident) and a NY (non-resident) state return.  And I figured it would be worth the extra cost to have software coordinate the returns.  Unfortunately, the numbers came out bizarre.  I ended up wading through the NJ and NY state websites for detailed instructions.  The NY instructions were confusing.  Fortunately, the NJ instructions had a clear explanation of the NJ forms and of how to deal with NY tax.  I needed to manually override some numbers in the NJ forms.  I decided to electronically file all the returns.  The federal filing went without a hitch.  The NY filing produced an error message that I needed to file by paper because of my particular filing scenario.  When I printed out the paper return, there was also a warning page stating that I was required to file electronically.  I mailed in the paper return with a note stating that I had tried to file electronically but it was rejected.  Keeping my fingers crossed.  I don’t hold H & R responsible for the issues with NY state electronic filing.  The NJ filing also produced an error message that I needed to file by paper because I had manually overridden some entries.  I do hold H & R responsible for the issues with NJ state electronic filing, because if the software had crunched the numbers properly, I wouldn’t have needed to manually override entries.  One minor gripe concerning paper filing of state returns.  Depending on your particular circumstances, you may need to include copies of certain federal forms with the state return.  With Turbotax, when you print the forms required for state filing, any required federal forms are automatically included.  With H & R, when you print the forms required for state filing, you get a checklist indicating that additional federal forms need to be printed.  You then need to manually select and print the required federal forms.  Note:  I don’t know whether Turbotax handles two state returns any better; as I mentioned, this was the first year I had to do that.  But I saw similar complaints in their reviews.

This review concerns only the download and installation experience for this product, Rosetta Stone Dutch, level 1, for Mac. As I use the product I might update this review.  As a Mac user, I'm accustomed to buying software on the App Store. Download and installation is automatic and fast. The download/install process for this product is as far from that experience as one could imagine. It's stunningly terrible, and I am not being hyperbolic.  First you need to download, mount, and launch Amazon's proprietary download software. What? In 2015?  Then, using Amazon's software, you download the product, which arrives in a disk image. You run the installer from the disk image, supplying your admin credentials.  Then you launch the software you bought, and rather than starting to use it, you are required to start updating. For me, I had to go through a sequence of two updates, each of which required download (each well over 100 MB), admin password entry, and acceptance of terms and conditions.  So, about 45 minutes in to this process (that's if you're lucky enough to have very fast broadband to accommodate the four downloads you've performed), you again try launching the product you bought. This time it does not prompt for yet another update. Yay? No. It asks you to insert your CD-ROM disk.  Of course, as a download product, there is no CD-ROM disk.  After trying various approaches to get around this problem, which included searching first on Amazon for help and then on the Rosetta Stone support pages for help, I was, one could say, well surprised but not delighted.  I then found, buried deep behind a labyrinth of unhelpful content on the Rosetta Stone site, a link to initiate a live chat session. Which I did. If the single star I've awarded indicates anything positive, it's that they do offer chat support, and it's available apparently any time of day.  The person who helped me was indeed able to help me solve the problem, but only because I could second guess his poor instructions. For example, he wrote "click" the the chat window when he meant "double click," and he asked me to move a file from a mounted disk image to the Desktop when that step is entirely unnecessary. In our chat, he wrote wonderfully ambiguous instructions such as "Please drag the file."  It turned out that to use the software I purchased, I had to use Finder to navigate to a hidden folder, create a new folder within it, name that folder with a particular case-sensitive name, and then drag a 400 MB file from the mounted, original disk image, into the folder I had manually created and named.  Then I could use the software.  Then I had to get past the mandatory registration process (of course, at this point I invented a name, email address, age, and so on, because the company had long since burned any remnant of trustworthiness). But I still couldn't use the program I'd purchased.  The running app then opened my web browser and sent me to an associated website, which prompted me, rather rudely, to install Adobe Flash. No. I just closed that Safari window, and then, back in the app, deselected the checkbox that had been selected by default to always send me to the web.  I wanted to learn a bit of Dutch. Instead I learned that this product, which is just level one of a multilevel sequence and which nominally costs more than a hundred dollars, has a 1995 style installation experience, and a horrible one even given that framing.  Wow.

I purchased this product for my brother, who did not need Outlook. Once installed, however, I realized that the software labels itself \\"Not for commercial use\\"--meaning, it's not licensed for use in a business, and this was going to be for use in an office. This was clearly my fault: I was only looking at the included products, and not thinking about the license terms.

No matter; I figured I would simply upgrade him to \\"Home and Business\\"--only to find that Microsoft's latest upgrade strategy is...well, there isn't one. According to Microsoft, this keeps things simpler for consumers, because apparently we were having trouble understanding the difference between \\"upgrade\\" and \\"full\\" versions. So to upgrade, you just have to buy the higher-level version at full price. As someone who has used Painter professionally since version 6, I must say I have mixed feelings about v2015. The previous version of Painter, X3, was, in my opinion, entirely unusable due to sluggishness in its pan, zoom, and tilt features. Corel appears to have fixed the input delay on the pan, which is good, but the zoom is still less responsive than it needs to be, and the tilt, while better than 13, is still sluggish. Compared to Photoshop and Manga Studio, Painter's pan/zoom/tilt are dreadfully slow.
I do like the responsiveness of the brush tracking, HOWEVER, the brush resizing, even if dropped back to \\"legacy\\" usage, is still unforgivably choppy and really impacts the speed at which you can work if you are getting into tight details and need to make rapid brush size changes. Also, many of the bugs that have plagued Painter since version 12 have yet to be addressed (such as the inability to rename a duplicate layer without deselecting it first and then re-selecting it, various things that lose the attention of the screen, disconnected reality where hotkeys are ignored, and require you to both select a brush and then click in the work area before you can do rapid-switch between the two working colors, loss of the main dropdown menu when switching back to Painter from another program, etc). In the end, it seems like v2015 is just a small group of fixes to solve the awfulness of X3, but all they have managed to accomplish is to make it OK to use. I still find myself going back to Painter 11 despite the crashiness of it. If you can get artistic brushes to do what you want in Photoshop or Manga Studio, I say go for those instead.

I tried Quicken many many years ago and decided I liked Microsoft Money better. But a few years ago, Money basically went into sunset mode and updates through MS Money were no longer possible. So I tried Quicken. So disappointing is the online capabilities of Quicken. While it's nice to at least have SOME accounts online-capable, what makes Quicken more disappointing than Microsoft Money is the fact that even the transaction files you download from various financial websites are simply not readable by Quicken, even though they are readable by Money, such as the QIF files. Money will import QIF files and OFX files easily. Quicken does not recognize either one. It seems to only recognize its own format, and if the website you use for handling finances doesn't have a specific Quicken file, you'll end up entering transactions manually or searching the internet for methods you can use to alter the downloaded transaction file to trick Quicken into importing the data anyway.

Quicken's reasoning for not allowing the normal import of any QIF file is highly annoying and it seems to have no point. They simply don't allow QIF data to be imported into credit accounts, while MS Money does.

I expected more than this from Quicken, especially after all these years. I expected it to be compatible with at least one format from every website that offers transaction downloads, even from the site itself as an import file, but this is not the case at all. I have more financial sites that are incompatible with Quicken than I had with MS Money. What a shame.

That said, Quicken's ability to generate reports seems more robust than MS Money. Money would not show how much available credit you have on credit cards, but Quicken does. The text reports in Quicken are not as fancy-looking as the ones in MS Money, so visually, Quicken's reports seem to be ONLY about the numbers.

The graphical user interface seems slow. While I have a 6-core AMDVishera CPU, a GeForce GTX 650, and 16 GB of RAM on an Asus Crosshair V Formula Z motherboard, Quicken's speed of redrawing the screen makes it look like it's running on an old 386 computer. Paying one bill from the Bill Reminder screen can take about three seconds to finally enter and change all the data on the screen.

Sometimes all transactions don't import into accounts. I've had a few instances where I've had to manually enter transactions I've downloaded because they didn't "register" into the Quicken account, yet they showed up on the statement.

Another minus to this is that during reconciliation of accounts, some of the items you need to check off won't show up in the reconciliation screen. If you switch back to your register, you see that the transaction is actually there. Apparently Quicken does you a "favor" and limits the transactions displayed in the reconciliation screen by using the date range of the statement you're reconciling. If a transaction in the Quicken register is outside the date of the statement, there's some special click procedure you have to use on the context menu for the entry to change some hidden date that does not appear in the register itself, but changing that date to something that's within the statement's date range makes the transaction available for reconciliation.

Overall, there are a lot of very stupid characteristics of this financial software that seem to have no point, such as the one I just described, that make this software annoying. The only reason to use it is if you want something current that'll download at least some of your transactions from within the software itself. If you've got something that works the way you want it to now, stick with it.

The lesson here is don’t just save your tax return in Intuit’s file format. Export it as a PDF, save AND print it for your records.

The second problem had to do with one form I needed not being ready. I started my taxes in early January and filled in details as the forms arrived. The warning that I couldn’t file because a particular form wasn’t ready yet kept coming up, and finally I started looking for help in the forums. I found an article posted by them which said the form in question was available for everything but E-File on Mac, and that it would be available for that final format on January 30th. I tried checking for updates and reinstalling as suggested but no luck. I was finally able to find a telephone number for customer service and speak to someone there after a 20-minute hold, only to be told they had no information other than what I knew from searching the forums, and no process for escalating my call to anyone who could help or even give me an updated ETA. I was promised a full refund for the software but have had to start all over on preparing my taxes and several weeks have gone by in which I could have already filed my return.

Intuit makes it hard to speak to anyone in the first place, and harder still to find anyone who can help you with your problems. Between that and the limited access to your own information that magically becomes no problem if you simply give them more money, I’m very dissatisfied.

Evidentia is the real deal. It is a groundbreaking program that gets it. Now genealogists that do research have a tool that supports the analysis and conclusion justification that they have been doing for years. The program lays out a simple path with support for each step of the way. Add a source, extract assertions (claims) from the source, analyse, draw a conclusion, document the conclusion. Evidentia can't force genealogists to use good methodology, but it does nudge them in the right direction.

I have been looking for this program for years. I have seen the problems conclusion based genealogy programs impose during the exploration and research portions of genealogy. I just didn't know what the program I wanted should look like. Now with Evidentia, I know.

I like that Evidentia encourages use of good citation habits with support for \\"Cite Your Sources\\" and good research habits encapsulated in \\"Genealogical Proof Standard\\".

Just as important as what is included in Evidentia, is what is left out. Ed did not try to make a do everything program and compete with all the conclusion based software out there. The many pretty tree programs have had years of development and evaluation and are very good at what they do. This `keep it as simple as possible, but no simpler' approach allowed a one man operation create something revolutionary.

Evidentia is a stand alone program and is useful as such. Users of the other genealogy programs and web sites can import people from their existing database and add the conclusions to their databases. Due to limitations with gedcom, moving the analysis and conclusion into other programs may take a little experimentation.

As for the software as implemented, it uses a desktop metaphor, that keeps the functionality in plain view, which especially helps beginners. The only problem I see with that is that it does restrict the work space a bit. For some functionality there are pop up boxesthat give more room. The always on top claim entry box is very useful.

I am pleased with the operation of the program and how it helps me with my genealogy process. Things will only get better as new features, reports and source templates are added and minor bugs fixed.

Outlook 2013 has what I consider to be a pleasant design (although I would prefer a much darker theme and more color choices) but lacks the connectivity for which I was hoping. I have two important e-mail accounts that I was hoping to use with this product: a personal Gmail account and a Microsoft Exchange account for my work, and that's where I ran into trouble.

In the case of the Gmail account, I was saddened to learn that Google and Microsoft disagree about the future of e-mail, calendar, and contact protocols and they're largely inoperable out of the box. I was able to configure e-mail by falling back to IMAP/SMTP but there are some known issues where Gmail accounts will slowly get out of sync and changes won't mirror to the server properly. For contacts, I found a free third-party program called GO Contact Sync Mod that was able to synchronize all of my contact information. I haven't found a solution for my Google calendar yet, but I believe there are some paid add-ins that might do the job. Even with add-ins, though, I would stay away until they fix the IMAP problems if you use Gmail.

For the Microsoft Exchange account, I was hoping it would be a breeze. Unfortunately, my workplace is stuck with Exchange 2003 and Outlook 2013 is not compatible. I'm sure it works fine with newer versions of Exchange, but I was surprised that it didn't just work for me because so many other apps do: even my phone is able to connect using the (apparently outdated) Exchange protocol. Outlook 2013 does support ActiveSync, but this is of no use because it explicitly blocks the connection to an Exchange server using ActiveSync. I've read this was for performance reasons, but I hate that they refuse to let me decide whether it's worth it or not (note that the Windows 8 mail program does work with it).

I also tried it with a Yahoo! and Outlook.com e-mail account and both worked to my satisfaction with the Outlook.com account having the best integrationof the ones I tried. I'm confident that if you're already using a newer version of Exchange or just Outlook.com for your e-mail, then you won't have the kinds of problems I've had. I can't recommend this product, though, as it fell far short of my expectations as a one-stop-shop for e-mail connectivity.

To keep this short and to the point, it does what it is supposed to. I'm running it on my Surface Pro 3 and it loads and runs like a charm. It's possible to create very nice layouts, but there are a few major things that Microsoft needs to implement in future versions of Publisher if it wants to be taken seriously. For starters, any publishing software worth anything should be able to automatically create certain parts of most books. A table of contents tool is not a feature in Publisher, nor is there the ability to create an index or glossary. That's a fairly major thing to leave out. Aside from that, there is no ability to add rounded corners to pictures. There is a workaround, treating pictures as a fill for a rectangle with rounded edges, but that's far less convenient. Along those same lines, there also needs to be better ability to adjust shapes such as rectangles and tweak their overall look. I'm sure this can be done somehow, because some of the templates Microsoft offers (a nice touch, by the way) have such things, but this brings me to my primary gripe with Publisher: there is no support available anywhere for it. If you want to know how to do anything, you're just going to have to figure it out yourself. Microsoft would do well to make a document explaining all of the features of this program - an actual user's manual. They could even make it in Publisher and it would turn out great.

In short, this program has all of the ability to duke it out with programs like InDesign, but it needs to have a few features added before that becomes a real possibility.
